principles.title: Scarcity narrows the mind
principles.motto: What you lack will eat your attention first.
principles.essence: Lack does not only empty your pocket; it narrows your mind. When money, time or food runs short, your attention tunnels onto the shortage and leaves less room for planning, patience and wisdom. So the first work of abundance is to win back a little slack, a small margin, so you can think again.
principles.depth: In their 2013 book Scarcity, the economist Sendhil Mullainathan and the psychologist Eldar Shafir argue that shortage of any kind captures the mind. They call this tunneling: what is scarce fills your view. Everything outside the tunnel (your health, your friendships, next year) fades. The cost falls on bandwidth, their word for the mental room we use to reason, plan and hold back impulses. Under strain we borrow at terrible rates, skip the clinic and snap at our children. We do this not because we are foolish but because the mind is full. This is why the poor so often pay a hidden tax of late fees and costly loans. Think of the five-six lender (borrow five, repay six), whose interest outruns any repayment. The findings are debated. Some later studies of payday cycles found smaller effects or none, so hold the size of the effect lightly. Philosophers saw the inward side long ago. Seneca wrote in his second letter to Lucilius, "It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor." Scarcity is both a condition of the purse and a habit of the mind. Both can be eased, one margin at a time.

tales.title: The Same Farmer, Twice
tales.who: Anandi Mani, Sendhil Mullainathan, Eldar Shafir, Jiaying Zhao, and the sugarcane farmers of Tamil Nadu
tales.where: Villupuram and Tiruvannamalai districts, Tamil Nadu, India
tales.source: Mani, Mullainathan, Shafir and Zhao, "Poverty Impedes Cognitive Function", Science 341 (2013)
tales.tale:
Before the harvest, the cane stands taller than a man, green and whispering in the wind, and the farmer who owns it is poor. The money is all out there in the field, locked inside the stalks. In the house, the rice tin is low. There are bangles pawned at the moneylender's. There is a loan, and the loan has a date.

After the harvest, the same farmer walks home from the sugar mill with the whole year's pay. Same man, same village, same hands. Only one thing has changed: for a little while, there is enough.

In the sugarcane country of Tamil Nadu, in southern India, four researchers saw in this a rare chance. Anandi Mani, Sendhil Mullainathan, Eldar Shafir and Jiaying Zhao knew that cane is cut once a year and paid for in one lump. So a family can be short of money for months and then, suddenly, flush. They did not need to compare rich people with poor people, who differ in a hundred ways. They could compare a person with himself.

So they visited several hundred farmers twice: once in the lean weeks before harvest, and once in the easier weeks after. Each time, the farmers did puzzles. One was a set of patterns with a missing piece, a common test of reasoning. Another showed colour names printed in the wrong colour of ink, and asked for the ink, a test of how well the mind holds back a quick wrong answer.

Before the harvest, the farmers did worse. Clearly worse. After the harvest, the same people, with the same schooling, solved more and stumbled less. The researchers checked other causes: tiredness, diet, the strain of the harvest work itself. The gap remained. The poverty was not in the men. It was on them, like a sack across the shoulders, and it pressed down on their thinking.

The study, published in the journal Science in 2013, was not the last word. Other researchers have since found smaller effects, or none, in other places and with other tests, and the argument goes on.

But the picture stays with you. A man in a green field, the same man as always, who thinks more clearly in the week the worry lifts.
tales.reveals: Scarcity is not a flaw of character but a load on the mind; the same person thinks better when the pressure eases. Building a little margin is not a luxury, because it gives you back your own intelligence.

tales.title: The Men Who Dreamed of Bread
tales.who: Ancel Keys and 36 volunteers, conscientious objectors in the Civilian Public Service
tales.where: Beneath the stands of Memorial Stadium, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, United States
tales.source: Ancel Keys and colleagues, The Biology of Human Starvation (1950); later interviews with the volunteers
tales.tale:
Under the stands of a football stadium in Minneapolis, in the cold of late 1944, thirty-six young men moved into a laboratory to go hungry on purpose.

They were conscientious objectors, men whose beliefs would not let them fight in the Second World War, and they wanted to serve some other way. A small booklet had asked them a question: "Will you starve that they be better fed?" Europe was starving. When the war ended, someone would have to feed millions of thin and broken people, and no one knew how best to do it. The scientist Ancel Keys meant to find out, by starving healthy men slowly and then bringing them back.

For three months they ate normally. Then, for six months, they ate about half of what their bodies needed: potatoes, turnips, dark bread, a little macaroni. They walked many miles each week. They lost about a quarter of their weight. Their hearts slowed. They shivered in summer.

But the strangest change was in their minds. Food took over their thoughts. The men read cookbooks the way other men read love letters. They collected recipes, studied menus, stared at pictures of meals. They chewed gum by the pack until the staff had to limit it. They cut their small portions into tiny pieces and ate them slowly, stretching every bite. Some dreamed of food at night. Several began to plan new lives as cooks. Their interest in friends, in news, in romance, simply faded, as if the whole world had shrunk to the size of a plate.

When the starving ended and they could eat again, many found they could not stop. Some ate far past fullness, and the hunger in their heads took months to leave, long after the hunger in their bodies was gone.

Keys and his team published the results in 1950, in two thick volumes called The Biology of Human Starvation. Relief workers and doctors learned from it, and it is still read by those who treat eating disorders. Such an experiment would not be allowed today.

The men gave their bodies to help the hungry. What they left the rest of us was a lesson about the mind: what you lack, you cannot stop seeing.
tales.reveals: Deprivation does not stay in the stomach; it climbs into attention, dreams and plans, and crowds out everything else. A mind gripped by want is not free to choose well. That is why easing scarcity, in food or money, is the ground every good decision stands on.

practice: For one day, jot down every money worry that crosses your mind and count them at night. Seeing the load on paper is the first step to lifting some of it off your mind.
Start a small buffer this week, even 200 pesos in a separate envelope or account. Then the next surprise cost will not throw you into the tunnel.
Make big money decisions (a loan, a large purchase, a job change) when you are rested and fed, never late at night or in a panic. Sleep on anything that can wait a day.
Simplify one recurring burden, such as a fixed day each month for paying bills, so it stops taking up space in your head.
principles.shadow: Fear of scarcity can become its own prison: hoarding, refusing to share, never feeling safe however much you hold. Aim for enough slack to think clearly, not a wall so high it shuts out the people you love.

principles.title: Wealth is made, not only taken
principles.motto: The pie is not fixed. Learn to bake.
principles.essence: Much of the world's wealth was not seized from someone else; it was created by people finding better ways to make what others need. If you see life as a fixed pie, you will spend it fighting over slices. If you see that value can be made, you start looking for ways to make more, and to share it.
principles.depth: Psychologists have a name for the instinct that one person's gain must be another's loss: zero-sum bias (Daniel Meegan, 2010). A survey across 37 countries by Joanna Rozycka-Tran and colleagues (2015) found the belief strongest where economies had grown least. It may be an echo of our ancestors' world, where land and game really were fixed. But economics, from Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776) onward, shows that specialisation and trade create value that did not exist before. Specialisation simply means each person doing the part they do best. David Ricardo's idea of comparative advantage (1817) adds a surprising twist. Two people can both gain from trade even when one is better at everything. Each can focus on what costs them least to give up. Paul Romer, who shared the 2018 Nobel prize in economics, showed why ideas are the great multiplier. A better recipe, unlike a barrel of oil, can be used by everyone at once without running out. None of this means everyone gains equally, or that no wealth is ever taken. Theft, fraud and exploitation are real, and growth can leave people behind. It means your surest path to wealth is usually to create value, not to grab it.

tales.title: Eighteen Steps and a Pin
tales.who: Adam Smith and the pin makers he described
tales.where: Kirkcaldy, Scotland, where Smith wrote; the workshop itself is unnamed
tales.source: Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776), Book I, Chapter 1
tales.tale:
A pin is a small thing. You can lose a hundred in a sewing basket and never miss one. But two and a half centuries ago a pin was made by hand. One Scottish thinker looked at that sliver of wire and saw in it the secret of the wealth of nations.

Adam Smith was a professor who went home to the quiet town of Kirkcaldy, by a grey sea, to write a book. It took him years. When it came out in 1776, it began not with kings or gold, but with a pin.

A worker making pins alone, Smith wrote, "could scarce, perhaps, with his utmost industry, make one pin in a day, and certainly could not make twenty." Think of it. He must draw out the wire, straighten it, cut it, sharpen it, make the head and fix it on, and polish the whole. Every step is done by the same tired hands.

But Smith described a small workshop where the work was divided. "One man draws out the wire, another straights it, a third cuts it, a fourth points it, a fifth grinds it at the top for receiving the head." The job was split into about eighteen steps. In this place, he said, ten workers, some doing two or three steps each, made "upwards of forty-eight thousand pins in a day." That is close to five thousand pins for each person, where alone each might have made one.

Nobody stole those pins. No one's share grew smaller. The extra pins simply came into being, out of better order, practised hands, and the time no longer lost in moving from task to task. Wealth had been made.

Historians note that Smith may have drawn his numbers from a French encyclopedia of crafts rather than from a visit of his own. And later in the same book he warned that a life spent on one tiny task could leave a worker's mind dull. He saw both sides.

Still, the lesson of the little pin has outlived him. When people work together, each growing skilled at a part, the world does not merely pass its wealth from hand to hand. It makes more.
tales.reveals: Specialisation and cooperation multiply what a group can produce, so wealth can grow without anyone being robbed. Smith's own warning about dulling work reminds you that how the pie grows matters as much as how big it gets.

tales.title: The Wager on Five Metals
tales.who: Julian Simon, economist; Paul Ehrlich, biologist, with John Harte and John Holdren
tales.where: United States
tales.source: John Tierney, "Betting on the Planet", New York Times Magazine (1990); Paul Sabin, The Bet (2013)
tales.tale:
Two clever men looked at the same world and saw opposite futures.

Paul Ehrlich was a biologist at Stanford, famous for a 1968 book called The Population Bomb. He believed the earth was running out: too many people, too few resources, hunger and shortage just ahead. Julian Simon was an economist at the University of Maryland, and he believed something that sounded almost foolish. People, he said, are not only mouths to feed but minds to think. When something grows scarce, its price rises, and the rising price sends human beings looking for more of it, or for something better.

In 1980 Simon offered a challenge. Pick any raw materials you like, he said. If their price, after inflation, goes up, you win. If it goes down, I win. Ehrlich and two colleagues, John Harte and John Holdren, took the bet. They chose five metals: chromium, copper, nickel, tin and tungsten. They imagined buying two hundred dollars' worth of each, a thousand dollars in all, and set the clock for ten years.

During that decade the world gained roughly eight hundred million people. Surely, it seemed, the metals would grow dear.

They did not. By 1990 all five had fallen in real price. Miners found new deposits. Engineers found ways to use less. Thin glass threads, made mostly from sand, began to carry telephone calls that copper wires once carried. In October 1990, Ehrlich mailed Simon a cheque for 576 dollars and seven cents, with no note inside, as Tierney reported.

It is an honest story only if you tell the rest. Economists who later checked other ten-year stretches of the twentieth century found that Ehrlich would have won in many of them; the 1980s were a lucky decade for Simon. And some treasures, like clean air, wild forests and a steady climate, carry no price in any market, so they can be used up quietly.

Still, the bet left a question that will not lie down. Is wealth a heap of stuff, slowly shrinking? Or is it, more often than we think, the work of human minds, which can grow?
tales.reveals: Prices and human ingenuity can turn shortage into invention, which is one way wealth is made rather than taken. The honest footnote, that the timing favoured Simon and some losses carry no price, keeps the lesson humble.

practice: List three ways you could make something better, faster or cheaper for the people your work serves; value created is the root of value earned.
Notice this week when someone else's success stings like your loss, and ask plainly: did they take this from me, or did they make it?
Try one trade of strengths with a friend or neighbour: you cook, they fix your phone; you tutor their child, they help with your paperwork. Notice how both of you come out ahead.
Begin learning one skill that combines with what you already know, since new combinations of ideas are where much new value comes from.
principles.shadow: Faith in a growing pie can blind you to real harm: growth that pollutes, exploits or leaves neighbours behind. Help the pie grow, and keep asking who gets a slice and what it costs the earth.

principles.title: Begin with what you have
principles.motto: Do not ask what you lack. Ask what is in your house.
principles.essence: Abundance rarely begins with a windfall. It begins when you stop staring at what is missing. Take honest stock of what you already hold: skills, people, tools, time, a small sum. Start there, use it fully, and more becomes possible.
principles.depth: The researcher Saras Sarasvathy studied expert entrepreneurs (2001). She found that most did not start with a grand goal and then hunt for resources. They started with what she called the bird in hand: who they are, what they know and whom they know. Then they asked what they could make from that. She named this way of working effectuation. Earlier, John Kretzmann and John McKnight (1993) urged poor neighbourhoods to map their assets, not only their needs. A list of needs invites people to wait for rescue, while a list of gifts invites them to act. Psychology offers a reason this matters. Staring at gaps feeds the scarcity mindset of the first principle. Counting resources builds what Albert Bandura (1977) called self-efficacy: the belief that you can act. That belief strongly predicts whether people try at all. The Stoic teacher Epictetus opened his Enchiridion (his handbook) by dividing the world into what is up to us and what is not. He told his students to begin with the first. None of this says the gaps are imaginary, or that poverty is merely a matter of attitude. It says the first step is always taken from where you stand.

tales.title: The Widow's Jar of Oil
tales.who: The prophet Elisha; a widow and her two sons
tales.where: Ancient Israel
tales.source: The Bible, 2 Kings 4:1 to 7 (King James Version)
tales.tale:
Her husband was dead, and his debt was still alive. He had been one of the young men who followed the prophets of Israel, a man who feared God, she said. But he left her no money, only a creditor, the man to whom the debt was owed. And the creditor was coming to take her two sons as bondmen, servants who would work until the debt was paid. In that world, a debt could swallow a child.

She ran to the prophet Elisha and cried out to him. And Elisha did not begin with a miracle. He began with two questions. "What shall I do for thee? tell me, what hast thou in the house?"

It is a hard question when you are poor. The honest answer feels like nothing. "Thine handmaid hath not any thing in the house," she said, and then, because she was honest, she finished the sentence: "save a pot of oil." Save a pot of oil. Not nothing, then. Something small, almost forgotten in a corner.

Elisha told her to go to all her neighbours and borrow empty vessels, jars and bowls and jugs. "Borrow not a few," he said. Then she was to go inside with her sons, shut the door, and pour her little oil into the borrowed vessels, one by one.

So she did. The neighbours lent what they had. The door closed. In the dim room her sons carried the jars and she poured, and the oil kept coming. Jar after jar filled, until she said to her son, "Bring me yet a vessel," and he answered, "There is not a vessel more." And the oil stayed. It stopped when the jars ran out, and not before.

She went back to Elisha, and he told her, "Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt, and live thou and thy children of the rest."

Believers read it as a miracle, others as a parable. Either way, notice its order. First, name what you have, however small. Then gather help from those around you. Then work, steadily, behind a closed door. In the end the oil was measured not by the jar she started with, but by the vessels she was willing to bring.
tales.reveals: Elisha's first question turns the widow from her lack to her one small asset, and from there to her neighbours. Abundance begins with naming what is in your house and preparing room for it to grow.

tales.title: The Soup Made from a Stone
tales.who: Hungry travellers and the people of a village (the tale has many tellers and no named author)
tales.where: Across Europe, from Portugal and France to Sweden and Russia
tales.source: European folk tradition, with versions such as Nail Soup (Sweden) and Axe Porridge (Russia)
tales.tale:
The travellers came over the hill at dusk, three of them, thin as fence posts, an empty pot knocking against one man's back.

The village saw them coming. Doors shut. Shutters closed. In every house, people hid what they had: a sack of potatoes under the bed, carrots in the cellar, a bit of salted meat up in the rafters. Times were hard, and strangers were trouble. When the travellers knocked and asked for food, every house gave the same answer. "We have nothing. We barely have enough for ourselves."

So the travellers went to the village square. They built a fire. They filled their pot with water from the well. And then, slowly, with great care, one of them took a smooth grey stone from his pocket and dropped it in.

A child came to watch. Then her mother. "What are you making?" "Stone soup," said the traveller. "It is very fine. Though it would be finer with a little salt." The woman went home and came back with salt. "Ah, and an onion would make it a soup fit for a wedding." Someone found an onion. A man remembered a few carrots. Another brought potatoes, another a cabbage, another, a little ashamed, a piece of meat. Each gave only one small thing: the thing they had said they did not have.

By dark the whole village was in the square, and the pot smelled like a feast. They ate together, and there was enough for everyone, and some to spare. Someone found a fiddle. The travellers were given beds. In the morning, as the story often ends, the villagers begged to buy the magic stone.

The tale is told all over Europe, and no one knows who told it first. In Sweden it is a nail that goes into the pot; in Russia, an axe; elsewhere, a button. The trick is always the same, and so is the truth inside it.

The village was never poor. It was only divided, each house counting its own small hoard and calling it nothing. The stone was worth nothing at all. What it did was coax the first person to say: I have something. The wealth was in the village all along, waiting for someone to begin.
tales.reveals: What looks like scarcity is often wealth that has not yet been gathered. One small, visible start can draw out the hidden gifts of a whole community.

practice: Make an "oil in the house" inventory: list your skills, tools, savings, contacts and free hours, and keep adding to it all week.
Choose one item from that list and put it to work this week to earn, save or help. Offer a skill for a fee, rent out an unused tool, or cook for a neighbour who will pay.
Like the travellers, start something small that invites others in, such as a paluwagan (a rotating savings circle), a shared garden or a study group. See what people bring.
Journal on this: "If I could never get more than I have right now, what would I build with it?"
principles.shadow: Counting what you have can slide into telling others, especially the poor, that their lack is only a matter of attitude. Begin with your own jar, and when you are able, be the neighbour who lends the vessels.

principles.title: Serve many, and wealth follows
principles.motto: Solve a real problem for many people, and money finds its way home.
principles.essence: In a fair exchange, money is a kind of thank-you note: people pay you because you made their lives better. The more people you truly serve, and the better you serve them, the more wealth tends to flow your way. Look first for the need, then for the reward.
principles.depth: Adam Smith wrote in 1776 that "it is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest." The deeper point is this: in a fair market, the baker's interest is served only by serving you. Peter Drucker put it plainly in The Practice of Management (1954): the purpose of a business is to create a customer. Serving workers well can serve a firm too. The economists Daniel Raff and Lawrence Summers (1987) studied Henry Ford's five-dollar day. They concluded that it really did raise productivity and cut quitting. Economists call this efficiency wages: paying more so that people work better and stay longer. Psychology adds that people who see whom their work helps often try harder. In a study led by Adam Grant (2007), university fundraising callers met a student who had been helped by their work. Later they raised far more money, though such effects vary from place to place. Yet serving many is no guarantee. Luck, timing, capital and connections matter greatly, and some people grow rich by harming many. That is why honesty must stand beside service, or it is not service at all.

tales.title: Five Dollars in the Snow
tales.who: Henry Ford, his partner James Couzens, and the workers of the Highland Park plant
tales.where: Highland Park, Detroit, Michigan, United States
tales.source: Detroit newspapers, January 1914; Henry Ford, My Life and Work (1922); Raff and Summers, Journal of Labor Economics (1987)
tales.tale:
On a freezing January morning in 1914, thousands of men stood outside a car factory near Detroit, stamping their feet in the snow, because of one number: five dollars.

The factory was Ford's plant at Highland Park, where the Model T, the plain black car for ordinary people, crept down a moving assembly line. The line was a wonder. It was also a misery. The work was fast and dull, the same motion again and again, and men quit in great numbers. In 1913 the company had to hire several workers for every one it managed to keep. Every new man had to be trained, and every untrained man slowed the line.

On 5 January 1914, Henry Ford and his partner James Couzens announced something no one expected. Most workers would now earn five dollars for an eight-hour day, roughly double the usual pay, for a shorter day than before. Newspapers across the country carried the story. Some business owners called it madness.

The men came at once. Within days the crowd at the gates was so large that, on a bitterly cold morning, the company turned fire hoses on them, and the water froze on their coats. It is not a pretty part of the story, and it should be told.

Nor was the money simple. Much of it came as a share of profits, paid only to workers who passed the checks of Ford's Sociological Department. Its inspectors visited homes to judge drinking, cleanliness and family life. Women at first did not qualify. The gift came with a watchful eye.

And yet the plan worked. Workers stayed. They learned their jobs well. Fewer quit, fewer missed days, and the line ran faster. In his 1922 book, Ford wrote that the five-dollar day "was one of the finest cost-cutting moves we ever made." Over the following years the price of a Model T kept falling, and many of the men who built the car could at last afford to buy one.

Ford had many faults, some of them ugly, and this was never pure kindness. But he had stumbled on a plain truth: serve your workers and your buyers better, and both may come back to you, again and again.
tales.reveals: Paying people well and making a product many could afford created a circle in which service returned as profit. The fire hoses and the home inspections remind you that service mixed with control is only half a virtue.

tales.title: Twenty-Seven Dollars in Jobra
tales.who: Muhammad Yunus, economics professor; Sufiya Begum and other villagers of Jobra
tales.where: Jobra, a village beside Chittagong University, Bangladesh
tales.source: Muhammad Yunus, Banker to the Poor (1999); Banerjee, Karlan and Zinman, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics (2015)
tales.tale:
The stool was made of bamboo, woven by hand, and it was beautiful. The woman who made it earned almost nothing for it.

In 1976 Muhammad Yunus was a young economics professor at Chittagong University in Bangladesh. Only two years earlier, a terrible famine had swept the country. In his classroom he taught elegant theories. Outside the campus walls, in the village of Jobra, people were hungry, and the theories did not seem to reach them.

So he walked into the village and began to ask questions. He met a woman named Sufiya Begum, who wove bamboo stools. She had no money to buy bamboo, so she borrowed from a trader, and the trader made her sell him every stool at the price he chose. After a long day's work, as Yunus tells it, she kept about two cents. She was not poor because she was lazy. She was poor because the small sum she needed came with chains.

Yunus asked a student to help him list everyone in Jobra caught in the same trap. When they finished, there were forty-two names, most of them women, by his account. He added up what they all needed to break free. The total came to about twenty-seven dollars.

Twenty-seven dollars. He later wrote of his shame at belonging to a society that could not supply so small a sum. So he lent it from his own pocket, and told them to repay when they could sell their goods at a fair price. As he tells it, they repaid.

From that small loan grew, over years of trial and error, the Grameen Bank, whose name means village bank. It lent tiny sums, mostly to poor women, often in small groups who stood by one another. Millions borrowed. In 2006 Yunus and the bank shared the Nobel Peace Prize.

The full story is more mixed than the legend. Careful studies in six countries, published together in 2015, found that small loans helped some borrowers grow their businesses. But they rarely lifted whole communities out of poverty, and some lenders who copied the idea charged cruel rates. Yet the first insight stands. There was value waiting in Jobra, in skilled hands. Yunus found a way to serve it, and the serving spread.
tales.reveals: Great value can lie hidden among people the market ignores, and serving them well can be both a kindness and a sound business. The mixed evidence teaches that no single tool rescues everyone, and that service turns sour when the terms turn cruel.

practice: Write down three problems people around you often complain about, in your barangay, your office or your family group chat. Ask which one you could help solve.
This week, ask two customers, clients or co-workers: "What could I do that would make your work or life easier?" Then do one thing they say.
Estimate the value you create, not only the pay you receive. How much time, money or worry do you save the people you serve each month?
If you employ anyone, even a household helper or a part-time assistant, find one way to treat them better this month, and notice what returns.
principles.shadow: "Serve many" can be twisted into "reach many at any cost": selling cheap things that harm, or squeezing workers to please customers. Serve truly, deal honestly, and measure success by lives improved, not only units sold.

principles.title: Plant trees you will not sit under
principles.motto: Plant today; the shade belongs to someone you may never meet.
principles.essence: The deepest wealth grows on a long clock. Think of savings that compound (earn returns on their returns), skills that deepen, trust that builds, and families and institutions that outlast you. When you think in decades instead of days, small steady choices become powerful. Plant some things you will not live to harvest.
principles.depth: Behavioural economists, who study how people really handle money, have shown that we discount the future steeply and unevenly. In other words, we treat later rewards as worth far less than they are. David Laibson (1997) modelled this present bias. A reward today feels far larger than a bigger one next year, yet we keep expecting our future selves to be patient. Hal Hershfield and colleagues (2011) showed people aged images of their own faces. Afterwards those people chose to set aside more for retirement, as if meeting their future self made that person real. Walter Mischel's famous marshmallow studies (from the late 1960s) suggested that children who could wait did better later in life. But a larger study by Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan (2018) found the link much weaker once family background was counted. It is a reminder that patience comes easier when life is stable. Philosophy supplies the wider frame. Edmund Burke, in Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790), described society as a partnership "between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born." Long-view wealth is that partnership in practice. You receive gifts from those who came before, and you pass them forward to people you will never meet.

tales.title: The Man Who Slept Seventy Years
tales.who: Honi the Circle-Drawer (Honi HaMe'agel); an old man planting a carob tree
tales.when: Set in the 1st century BC; written down centuries later
tales.where: The land of Israel
tales.source: Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 23a
tales.tale:
An old man knelt in the dry earth, pressing a seedling into the ground. A traveller stopped to watch.

The traveller was Honi, a holy man people called the Circle-Drawer. Once, in a year of drought, as the tale goes, he drew a circle in the dust, stepped inside, and told God he would not leave it until rain came. And the rain came. He was a man who liked answers.

So he asked the old man a question. "How long until this tree gives fruit?" It was a carob tree, whose dark pods are sweet and feed both goats and the poor. "Seventy years," said the old man. "And are you sure you will live seventy more years?" The old man did not stop working. He said, as the Talmud records it, "I found the world full of carob trees. As my fathers planted for me, so I plant for my children."

Honi walked on, and when he grew tired he sat down to eat his bread. Sleep came over him, the story says, and a ring of rock rose around him and hid him from sight, and he slept for seventy years.

When he woke, he saw a man gathering pods from a great carob tree. "Are you the one who planted this?" Honi asked. "No," said the man. "I am his grandson." Then Honi understood how long he had slept. He went home and asked for his son. His son was dead. He went to the house of study, where scholars argued over the law, and heard them say, "Our learning is as clear as in the days of Honi the Circle-Drawer." "I am Honi," he said. They did not believe him. No one knew him, and no one gave him honour.

Honi had been a great man in his own time, and he slept through the time that came after. Grieving and alone, he prayed for death, and it came. The teacher Rava said of him: "Either friendship or death."

It is a legend, told by teachers long after Honi lived. But read it twice and you see who the true hero is. Not the famous man who slept. The nameless one on his knees, who planted for people he would never see.
tales.reveals: Wealth that crosses generations depends on people willing to plant without expecting to harvest. The tale also warns that a life slept through, however famous, leaves no shade and no friends behind.

tales.title: The Temple Builders of Fourteen Centuries
tales.who: Kongo Shigemitsu, the Kongo family and their carpenters; Prince Shotoku
tales.where: Osaka, Japan
tales.source: Kongo Gumi's own company history; news reports on its 2006 takeover; records of Shitenno-ji temple
tales.tale:
In the year 578, a carpenter crossed the sea from Korea to Japan, carrying the skill of his hands.

His name, as the company's history records it, was Kongo Shigemitsu. He came from the kingdom of Baekje, where Buddhist temples were built with great art. As the story is told, he was invited by Prince Shotoku, who wished to raise a great temple in what is now Osaka. The temple was Shitenno-ji. Its wooden beams were joined so cleverly that they held together with little need for nails.

Then his family kept building. Generation after generation, the Kongo family and its carpenters, the firm called Kongo Gumi, built and mended temples and shrines. Shitenno-ji itself burned and fell many times over the centuries: to lightning, to war, to the bombs that fell on Osaka in 1945. Again and again, Kongo builders helped raise it up. Their saws and chisels passed from one generation to the next. When a son was not fit to lead, the family often adopted a capable son-in-law to carry the name. They chose skill over birth order, so the craft would not die.

The company has long spoken of a family scroll from the Edo period, said to hold rules for later leaders. Keep to the work you know, live modestly, care for your craftsmen. Whether every line is as old as claimed is hard to say. But the spirit fits a house that lived for centuries by doing one thing well.

For more than fourteen hundred years, through emperors and warlords, fires and earthquakes, the family endured. Kongo Gumi is often called the oldest independent company the world has known.

Then came the 1980s, when land prices in Japan rose like a fever. The company borrowed heavily and bought land, stepping outside its craft. When the bubble burst, the land lost value, the debts remained, and fewer people paid for new temples. In 2006, unable to carry its debts, Kongo Gumi was taken over by a larger builder, the Takamatsu Construction Group. It lives on inside that group, its carpenters still raising temples.

The lesson cuts both ways. Fourteen centuries were built on patience, craft and care for the next generation. A few hurried years of borrowing nearly undid them all.
tales.reveals: Lasting wealth comes from patience, deep skill and careful succession, choosing the most able heir over the convenient one. It also shows how quickly a short-term gamble with borrowed money can undo what centuries built.

practice: Write a letter to yourself twenty years from now describing what you hope to have built. Reread it whenever you are tempted to trade the long for the short.

Plant one "carob tree" this week. Open a long-term savings plan, such as Pag-IBIG MP2 (a government savings scheme some Filipinos use). Or begin a skill you will practise for years, or simply plant a real tree.
Ask the oldest person in your family what someone once planted for them, in land, schooling, savings or values. Write the answer down for the next generation.
Before any big purchase or loan, ask "How will this look in ten years?" and wait one full day before you decide.
principles.shadow: The long view can sour into endless waiting. You may sacrifice for years with no joy today, or make plans so distant you neglect the people beside you now. Plant for tomorrow, and also share some fruit with those you love today.

principles.title: Become hard to replace
principles.motto: Learn a craft so well that the world comes looking for you.
principles.essence: Your first and most lasting capital is what you can do. Choose a skill that others truly need, and practise it until you are among the best you know. Keep learning, so that no machine and no cheaper hand can easily take your place.
principles.depth: Economists call skill human capital: the earning power you carry in your head and hands. Gary Becker, in Human Capital (1964), showed that training behaves like an investment. It costs time now and pays an income for decades, and unlike money in a drawer, no thief can take it. Adam Smith had already noted in The Wealth of Nations (1776) that a skilled worker's wage must repay the long years of learning. That is part of why rare skills earn more. Psychology shows how skill grows. K. Anders Ericsson, Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Romer (1993) found that the best young violinists had spent far more hours in deliberate practice. That means focused work on weak points, with feedback, just beyond comfort. A later meta-analysis, a study that pools many studies (Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald, 2014), found practice explains less of the difference than Ericsson claimed. So talent, timing and luck matter too. Still, nobody becomes rare without practice. Aristotle said it plainly in the Nicomachean Ethics: we become builders by building. Being hard to replace rarely means one skill alone. More often it is a combination few people hold, like a nurse who can code or a cook who can keep accounts. And craft feeds the soul as well as the purse. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's research on flow (being fully absorbed in a task) found people are often happiest when stretched by work they do well.

tales.title: The Washtub and the Tin
tales.who: Sarah Breedlove, later Madam C. J. Walker, and her daughter Lelia (later A'Lelia)
tales.where: Delta, Louisiana; St. Louis; Denver; Indianapolis
tales.source: Walker's 1912 speech to the National Negro Business League; A'Lelia Bundles, On Her Own Ground (2001)
tales.tale:
Picture a tub of grey water, steam rising, and a young woman's arms red to the elbow. The clothes belong to other people. The wage, about a dollar and a half a day as the accounts give it, belongs to rent and bread. Her name is Sarah Breedlove, and she is scrubbing so that her daughter can go to school.

She was born in 1867 on a cotton plantation in Delta, Louisiana, the first child in her family born free. Her parents had been enslaved. By seven she was an orphan, by fourteen a wife, by twenty a widow with a little girl named Lelia. She went upriver to St. Louis, where her brothers worked as barbers, and she took in laundry. For close to twenty years, the washtub was her world.

Then her hair began to fall out. Many Black women of her time suffered the same, from poor food, harsh soaps and homes without running water. Sarah began to test remedies on her own scalp. For a while she sold hair products for Annie Turnbo Malone, another Black businesswoman, and she watched closely how a product was made, explained and sold. She was learning a craft while she lived it.

In 1905 she moved to Denver, cooked for a pharmacist by day, as the story is told, and mixed her own formula at night. She married a newspaperman, Charles Joseph Walker, and took the name Madam C. J. Walker. Then she went door to door, washing and treating women's hair in their own kitchens, showing rather than telling.

Here is what made her hard to replace. Anyone could copy a tin of ointment. Few could copy what she built around it: a method, a training school, and thousands of agents, mostly Black women. They learned the work and earned far more than any washtub paid. By 1910 she had a factory in Indianapolis.

In 1912 she stood before the National Negro Business League and spoke in words still on record. She told them she had come from the cotton fields, been promoted to the washtub and then the kitchen, and then promoted herself into business.

She died in 1919. She is often called America's first self-made woman millionaire, though her estate may have been somewhat less. No one disputes the larger fortune she left behind: thousands of women who had learned to stand on their own skill.
tales.reveals: Walker's product could be copied; her skill, her method and the network of trained women she built could not. Being hard to replace often means mastering not one task but the whole craft around it: making, teaching and selling.

tales.title: Three Years and a Day
tales.who: A journeyman carpenter (a composite figure) and the masters who take him in
tales.when: Since the late Middle Ages; still practised today
tales.where: German-speaking Europe
tales.source: The guild custom of the Wanderjahre or Walz, as described in craft histories; the carpenter is a composite
tales.tale:
At the edge of a small German town, a young man in black stands by the sign that marks the town line. His trousers are wide corduroy, his hat broad, his whole life tied in one cloth bundle on a twisted walking stick. Behind him is his mother's kitchen. He will not see it again for three years and a day.

He is not one real person. He is a composite, drawn from a custom that is real and old. In the guilds of German-speaking Europe, the brotherhoods that ruled each trade, a boy first served as an apprentice, sweeping shavings and learning the names of tools. When he passed his test he became a journeyman. The word comes from the French journee, a day: he was paid by the day. Now he had to wander. The Germans call these the Wanderjahre, the wander years, or simply the Walz.

The rules, as many brotherhoods still keep them, are strict. Walk, or ride with strangers, and by tradition never pay for travel. Do not come within about fifty kilometres of home. Arrive at a workshop, knock, and ask for work in the old formal words. Work for food, a bed and a little pay, then move on.

So our carpenter learns. In one valley the roofs are steep for snow, and he learns to cut them. In a harbour town he learns how salt eats wood. One master is slow and exact, another fast and rough, and from both he learns what to do and what never to do. Each town presses its stamp into his travel book, a record of where he has worked.

When he comes home, he is not the boy who left. He has seen a dozen ways to join a beam. Now he can make a piece of work for the masters to judge, his masterpiece, which is where that word comes from. If it passes, he may open his own shop and take apprentices of his own.

The custom nearly died in the twentieth century, but it survives. Some hundreds of journeymen, women among them now, still walk the roads in their black clothes, though no one keeps an exact count. They carry no map of shortcuts, only the slow road and their hands.

Skill, the old guilds knew, is not poured into you. You walk to it.
tales.reveals: The wander years show that mastery comes from range as well as repetition: many masters, many problems, many places. A worker who has seen a dozen ways to do a thing is far harder to replace than one who knows only his own village's way.

practice: Name the one skill that most decides your income. Spend thirty focused minutes on it four days this week, aimed at your weakest point, not your favourite part.
Ask someone better than you to watch your work and name one thing to fix. Thank them, and fix it before the week ends.
List two or three abilities you have that rarely appear together (for example English, Bisaya and bookkeeping). Ask yourself who needs exactly that combination.
Take a small wander year: this month, watch or visit three people in your field who work differently from you, and borrow one method from each.
principles.shadow: Craft goes wrong when it hardens into pride: refusing to teach, scorning new methods, or polishing one skill long after the world has stopped needing it. Keep learning, and keep passing on what you know, as Walker did.

principles.title: Own something
principles.motto: Wages pay for your hours; what you own keeps working while you rest.
principles.essence: A wage buys your time once. Ownership, of a business, a share, a piece of land or the rights to your own work, can keep earning long after the hour is spent. Aim, step by careful step, to own at least part of what your effort builds.
principles.depth: Economists divide income into returns to labour and returns to capital, the things you own. Thomas Piketty wrote Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2013). He argued that across long stretches of history the return on capital has often grown faster than wages. So those who own tend to pull ahead of those who only work. His data and conclusions are hotly debated, but few dispute that owners gain most in good decades. John Locke, in his Second Treatise of Government (1690), grounded property in labour: when you mix your work with something, it becomes yours. Ownership also changes how people behave. Research on psychological ownership (Pierce, Kostova and Dirks, 2001) found that people who feel something is theirs take better care of it. The IKEA effect (Norton, Mochon and Ariely, 2012) shows we value what we helped to build. There is a trap here too. The endowment effect (Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler, 1990) makes us overprize what we already hold, so we cling to bad assets. And owning carries risk that a wage does not: a business can fail, a price can fall. Wise ownership therefore starts small and spreads out. Think of a cooperative share, a side business or the rights to your own designs or writing. Or think of a modest stake in a broad fund (one that holds many companies at once), or a plot that can feed you.

tales.title: The Rights Nobody Wanted
tales.who: George Lucas and 20th Century Fox, under its head of film Alan Ladd Jr.
tales.where: Los Angeles, California
tales.source: Interviews with Lucas and film trade reporting; the dollar figures vary between accounts
tales.tale:
Imagine an office in Los Angeles, a contract lying open on the table, and a young bearded man who has just made a hit. It is 1973. His film American Graffiti, a cheap little story about teenagers cruising cars on one summer night, is filling cinemas. George Lucas is twenty-nine, and he has a strange idea about knights in space.

The studio, 20th Century Fox, has agreed to let him make it. Now comes the talk of money. After a hit, a director is expected to ask for more. Lucas could have pressed for a much bigger fee, several hundred thousand dollars more by most accounts. He did not. He asked for something else.

He asked to keep the rights to any sequels. And he asked to keep the merchandising rights: the right to make and license toys, shirts, lunchboxes, anything that carried the film's names and pictures. To the studio this looked like a cheap trade. Film merchandise rarely earned much in those days. Who would buy a toy of a robot nobody had heard of? Fox, guided by Alan Ladd Jr., agreed. The figures change from one retelling to the next, but the shape of the deal does not.

Lucas has said that money was not his first thought. He wanted control, so that no studio could cut his story to pieces or stop it halfway. Ownership was how he kept the future of his own work in his own hands.

Star Wars opened in May 1977, and the lines wrapped around city blocks. The toy maker Kenner had so little time that, for Christmas, it sold an empty box: a certificate promising the figures would arrive in spring. Children wanted it anyway.

The toys, the books, the games, the sequels: over the years they earned far more than the first film itself. With that income Lucas built his own company, Lucasfilm, and its workshops for sound and special effects. In 2012 he sold Lucasfilm to Disney for about four billion dollars.

It began with a choice that looked foolish to the sensible people in the room: a bigger wage, once, or a piece of whatever might grow. He took the piece, and he took the risk with it. Had the film failed, those rights would have been worth nothing at all.
tales.reveals: Lucas traded a one-time payment for a share of whatever his work would become. Ownership let him earn for decades and, more than that, decide his work's future. But it paid only because he also carried the risk of failure.

tales.title: Butter, Sugar, Flour and Oatmeal
tales.who: The Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers, a group of weavers and other working men
tales.where: 31 Toad Lane, Rochdale, Lancashire, England
tales.source: George Jacob Holyoake, Self-Help by the People: History of Co-operation in Rochdale (1858)
tales.tale:
On a winter evening in 1844, on a narrow street called Toad Lane, a shop door opens for the first time. It is almost the shortest day of the year. Inside, by the light of candles, there are only a few sacks and tubs: butter, sugar, flour and oatmeal. Outside, some local boys have gathered to jeer.

The men behind the counter are weavers and other working men of Rochdale, a mill town in the north of England. Times are hard. Wages are low and many shops cheat them. Flour is mixed with chalk, butter with cheaper fat, and the scales are often false. The shopkeeper owns the shop, so the shopkeeper sets the price.

So the men asked a simple question: what if we owned the shop ourselves? For months they saved, a few pennies a week, until about twenty-eight of them had put in a pound each. That is how the story is usually told; the exact count is disputed. With that small heap of coins they rented the ground floor of an old warehouse, bought their first stock, and named themselves the Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers.

They wrote down rules, and the rules were the real treasure. Anyone could join. Each member had one vote, however much he had put in. Goods would be pure and weights honest. Sales would be for cash, so no one sank into debt. And the profit would not go to one owner: it would be paid back to members according to how much each had bought. This was the dividend, which Lancashire families came to call, fondly, the divi.

The boys stopped laughing. Within a few years the society had hundreds of members, and in time thousands. It added a library and a reading room. Its rules were copied across Britain, then the world. Cooperatives today, from farmers' groups to credit cooperatives in the Philippines, still trace much of their thinking to those Rochdale principles.

None of these men was rich. Not one could have bought a shop alone. But together they could own one, and owning it changed everything: the price, the quality, and where the profit went.

A few sacks of oatmeal, a pound apiece, and a door opened in the darkest week of the year. The light, it turned out, was only beginning.
tales.reveals: The Pioneers could not afford to own alone, so they owned together, and ownership let them set honest prices and keep the profit among themselves. Ownership is not only for the rich: pooled savings and fair rules can make owners of ordinary people.

practice: List what you own that earns or could earn: skills you could teach, tools, land, shares, a stall. If the list is empty, that is your starting line, not a shame.
Before you sign any job offer, freelance contract or partnership, read who owns what you create. Ask for a share, a royalty or the rights back, even if the answer is no.
Find a credit or consumer cooperative near you. Before you decide whether to join, read its rules on membership, votes and dividends (profits paid back to members).
Start one small thing you own outright this month, such as a sari-sari corner, a set of designs or a short course you teach. Keep it modest, and keep its money separate.
principles.shadow: Ownership turns sour when it becomes grasping. It squeezes workers and partners, clings to a failing asset out of pride, or bets the family's rice money on one venture. Own with people you trust, start small, and remember that everything you own can also lose value.

principles.title: Multiply your effort
principles.motto: Find a longer lever, and a small push moves heavy things.
principles.essence: Effort alone grows slowly: one pair of hands, one day at a time. Leverage, through tools, systems, helpers, media or capital (money put to work), lets the same effort reach far more people. Look for the levers in your work, and respect the ones that can also break you.
principles.depth: In On the Equilibrium of Planes, Archimedes proved that two weights balance at distances in inverse proportion to their size. Put simply: with a long enough arm, a small force lifts a great load. Economics found the same law in human work. Adam Smith showed how the division of labour and machines multiply what each worker produces. The economics of information goods (Carl Shapiro and Hal Varian, Information Rules, 1999) adds a further point. A song, a book or a piece of software, once made, can be copied for almost nothing, so one person's effort can serve millions. Leverage comes in several kinds: tools, people (hiring or partnering), capital, and media such as writing, recordings and code. The mind struggles with multiplication. Studies of exponential growth bias (Wagenaar and Sagaria, 1975; Stango and Zinman, 2009) show the problem. People badly underestimate how fast multiplied things grow, whether gains or debts. Financial leverage means borrowing to invest, and it cuts both ways. It enlarges losses exactly as it enlarges gains, which is why so many fortunes built on debt collapse. The Pareto principle is named after Vilfredo Pareto's 1896 observation about land in Italy. It is a rough pattern, not a law, but it points the same way: a few of your actions likely produce most of your results. Find those, and lengthen their reach.

tales.title: A Place to Stand
tales.who: Archimedes of Syracuse and King Hiero II
tales.where: Syracuse, Sicily
tales.source: Plutarch, Life of Marcellus (c. AD 100); Pappus of Alexandria, Collection, Book 8 (c. AD 340)
tales.tale:
Down at the harbour of Syracuse, a ship lies on the sand. It is a big merchant ship with three masts, one of the king's own, and it took a crowd of men, sweating and shouting, to drag it there. Now it is loaded with cargo, and people stand on its deck. They wait. Across the sand, one man sits alone, holding the end of a rope.

The man is Archimedes, the greatest mathematician of the Greek world, and the king who watches is Hiero II, ruler of Syracuse in Sicily. This is how the Greek writer Plutarch tells it, about three centuries later, so we should hold the details lightly.

Archimedes had written to the king that with a given force, any weight at all could be moved. He even boasted, Plutarch says, that if there were another earth, he could go to it and move this one. Hiero, a practical man, asked him to prove it. Show me, said the king, a great weight moved by a small force.

So here they are. Archimedes has run the rope through a set of pulleys, wheels that turn the rope and share out the load. He does not strain. He sits, and pulls gently, hand over hand. And the ship, the heavy ship that took so many backs to haul, glides toward him over the sand as smoothly as if it were floating on calm water.

Later writers pressed the story into one bright line. Pappus of Alexandria, writing more than five hundred years after Archimedes died, gives him the saying: give me a place to stand, and I will move the earth. Whether Archimedes ever spoke those words, no one can be sure. But he had done the mathematics. In his book on balance, he proved the law of the lever: a small weight far from the pivot can balance a great weight near it.

What the king saw that day was not a strong man. It was a clever arrangement. The strength was the same plain strength of two arms. What changed was where it was applied, and how.

That is the whole secret, and it is both humble and enormous. You do not need to become a giant. You need a longer lever, and a place to stand.
tales.reveals: Archimedes moved the ship with ordinary strength placed in the right arrangement. Leverage is not working harder; it is finding the tool, system or position that lets the same effort do far more.

tales.title: The Press in Mainz
tales.who: Johannes Gutenberg, his lender Johann Fust, and Fust's partner Peter Schoeffer
tales.where: Strasbourg and Mainz, Germany
tales.source: Records of the 1455 lawsuit (the Helmasperger notarial record); Enea Silvio Piccolomini's letter of March 1455; the surviving Gutenberg Bibles
tales.tale:
In a monastery room, a scribe bends over a sheet of calfskin. His pen scratches. His candle gutters. To copy one Bible by hand might take him many months, perhaps more than a year. When he is done, there will be exactly one more Bible in the world.

Now step into a workshop in Mainz, Germany, around 1450. It smells of oil, hot metal and damp paper. A tall wooden press, built like the screw presses that squeeze grapes for wine, groans as two men pull its bar. They lift the sheet. A full page of Latin, black and even, shines up at them. They lay down another sheet and pull again.

The man behind it all is Johannes Gutenberg, a metalworker, not a priest or a scholar. Printers in China and Korea had used movable type centuries before. But Gutenberg put together a system suited to Europe's alphabet. A hand mould cast thousands of identical metal letters quickly, an oily ink clung to metal, and the press brought them together. Each letter could be set into words, used, broken apart and used again.

That was the lever. His hands were no faster than the scribe's. But arranged this way, their work could be repeated hundreds of times. By about 1455 his shop had finished a great Bible with 42 lines to a page, perhaps 180 copies, scholars estimate. A churchman named Enea Silvio Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, saw its pages at a fair in Frankfurt and wrote to a friend that they could be read without glasses.

But there was another lever in the room, and it was dangerous. To build all this, Gutenberg had borrowed heavily from a Mainz merchant, Johann Fust. In 1455 Fust sued for his money. Gutenberg lost, and much of his workshop and type passed to Fust and his partner, Peter Schoeffer, who went on printing with great success.

Gutenberg lived on, quieter. In his last years the Archbishop of Mainz granted him a yearly allowance of grain, cloth and wine. He died in 1468. By 1500, printing presses were at work in well over two hundred towns across Europe.

He had found the longest lever of his age. He had also learned, at great cost, that borrowed force pulls both ways.
tales.reveals: Gutenberg's press let one workshop's effort reach thousands of readers, a lever that changed the world. Yet his borrowing was a lever too, and it cost him his shop: multiply your effort, but know which levers can also multiply your losses.

practice: List the tasks you did last week and mark the ones only you could do. For each of the rest, ask whether a tool, a template, a helper or a checklist could carry it.
Turn one thing you explain again and again into something reusable: a written guide, a short video, a price list or a recipe card. Then your words work while you are elsewhere.
Learn one tool this week that multiplies your work. It might be a spreadsheet formula, a scheduling app, or a better way of buying stock in bulk for a small store.
Before borrowing to grow anything, write down what happens if your income falls by half for six months. If the answer is ruin, the lever is too long.
principles.shadow: Leverage goes wrong when you borrow beyond what a bad year could repay, or treat people as mere levers instead of partners. Multiply your effort with tools and fair dealing, and keep debts small enough that one storm cannot sink you.

principles.title: Opportunity wears work clothes
principles.motto: Before you sell the farm, dig in your own backyard.
principles.essence: Most opportunities do not arrive gift-wrapped. They hide in ordinary problems close to you: in complaints, in things that keep breaking, in needs nobody has bothered to meet. Train your eyes to notice them, and your hands to do the plain work they ask.
principles.depth: The economist Israel Kirzner, in Competition and Entrepreneurship (1973), described enterprise as alertness: noticing a gain that others have overlooked, often lying in plain sight. Joseph Schumpeter stressed new combinations of things already known, and a rivet on a pocket is exactly that. Louis Pasteur told an audience at Lille in 1854 that in the fields of observation, chance favours only the prepared mind. Psychology adds a warning and a hint. The warning: we are drawn to the distant and the new. Research on maximising (Schwartz and colleagues, 2002) looked at people who always hunt for the best possible option. They tend to be less satisfied with what they choose. The hint comes from Richard Wiseman's experiments with people who called themselves lucky or unlucky (The Luck Factor, 2003). They suggested the lucky notice more because they are relaxed and open. In one test, people counted the photographs in a newspaper. Many anxious people missed a large printed message telling them the answer. His work is popular science, not a settled finding, so treat it as suggestive. A famous line says opportunity is missed because it is dressed in overalls and looks like work. It is usually credited to Thomas Edison, but no one has found the original. Its truth does not depend on who said it.

tales.title: The Farmer Who Sold His Diamonds
tales.who: Russell Conwell, and Ali Hafed, the farmer in his parable
tales.when: Parable; Conwell gave the lecture from the 1870s until 1925
tales.where: A farm near the River Indus (in the parable); Philadelphia and across the United States
tales.source: Russell H. Conwell, Acres of Diamonds (lecture, printed in several editions from 1890)
tales.tale:
A farmer sits by his fire in the evening, and a visitor tells him about diamonds. The visitor is an old Buddhist priest, and he speaks of stones like frozen drops of sunlight, so rare that a handful could buy a kingdom. The farmer's name is Ali Hafed. He has land, orchards, children and peace. That night, for the first time in his life, he goes to bed poor.

This is not history. It is a parable, a teaching story, made famous by Russell Conwell, an American minister. Conwell said an old guide told it to him while he travelled along the Tigris River in 1870. He retold it in a lecture called Acres of Diamonds, and he gave that lecture, by his own count, more than six thousand times.

In the story, Ali Hafed cannot rest. He sells his farm, leaves his family in a neighbour's care, and goes searching. He crosses mountains, deserts and seas. Years pass. His money runs out. At last, ragged and hopeless, on the shore at Barcelona in Spain, he throws himself into the waves and is gone.

Back home, the man who bought his farm leads his camel to drink at the garden stream. In the white sand he sees a flash: a black stone with a strange light inside it. He sets it on his shelf as a curiosity. When the old priest visits again, he cries out. It is a diamond. They run to the stream, dig with their fingers, and find more. In Conwell's telling, the farm became the great diamond mine of Golconda. That part is pure invention; the real mines of Golconda in India have their own history.

Conwell's lesson was simple. Before you run off to seek your fortune far away, look hard at where you stand: your street, your trade, the troubles of your neighbours. The diamonds, he said again and again, may be in your own backyard.

He did more than talk. Money from his lectures helped him build Temple University in Philadelphia, which began as night classes for working people too poor for other schools.

One caution. Conwell also preached that getting rich was close to a duty, and he spoke harshly of the poor, as if most poverty were their own fault. Take his diamonds. Leave that.
tales.reveals: The parable warns against the restless belief that fortune is always somewhere else. Opportunity is often hidden in ground you already know, waiting for someone patient enough to look closely and do the digging.

tales.title: Copper at the Corners
tales.who: Jacob Davis, a tailor in Reno, and Levi Strauss, a cloth merchant in San Francisco
tales.where: Reno, Nevada, and San Francisco, California
tales.source: US Patent No. 139,121 (20 May 1873); Levi Strauss and Co. company history
tales.tale:
In a tailor's shop in Reno, Nevada, a woman lays a pair of torn trousers on the counter. The pockets have ripped right off. Her husband, a labourer, keeps tearing them, she says, stuffing them with tools and the hard bits of hard work. Can the tailor make a pair that will last? The year, by the company's own history, is 1870.

The tailor is Jacob Davis, an immigrant from Riga, in Latvia, who had tried several trades in the American West before settling to his needle. He looks at the weak points: the corners of the pockets, the base of the fly, wherever the strain pulls hardest. Then his eye falls on something already in his shop. Copper rivets, the small metal studs he uses to fasten straps on horse blankets.

What if he hammered a rivet into each corner?

He tried it. The trousers held. Word went round among the working men, and soon they were asking for the riveted kind. Davis knew he had something, and he knew others would copy it. He needed a patent, the government paper that says an idea is yours for a time. But the fee was about sixty-eight dollars, a large sum for a small tailor.

So in 1872 he wrote to the man who sold him his cloth, Levi Strauss. Strauss was a Bavarian-born merchant who had come to San Francisco in 1853, in the gold rush years, to sell dry goods. Davis proposed a partnership: Strauss would pay for the patent, and they would share it. Strauss saw the sense. On 20 May 1873 they received patent number 139,121, for an improvement in fastening pocket openings. Davis moved to San Francisco to run the making. The trousers were cut from heavy cotton duck and from blue denim, and called waist overalls.

A popular legend says Strauss first made trousers from tent canvas for gold miners. No proof of that has been found. The true story is plainer, and better. There was no gold strike, no dream, no genius on a mountain. There was a complaint at a counter, a box of rivets on a shelf, and two men willing to do the work and share the reward.

The diamonds were in the shop all along.
tales.reveals: The riveted trousers came from taking a plain complaint seriously and joining two ordinary things already at hand. Opportunity often arrives as a problem someone brings you. It pays only when you are willing to do the paperwork, the partnering and the plain labour.

practice: For one week, write down every complaint you hear from customers, neighbours or coworkers. At the end, circle the one you could solve with skills or tools you already have.
Walk your own barangay or neighbourhood as if you were a visitor. Note what is missing, overpriced or done badly, and who would pay to have it done well.
Test one small idea for less than a thousand pesos, or the equivalent where you live, before quitting anything or borrowing anything.
Journal on this question: what am I treating as far away that might be close at hand? Write the honest answer, even if it is uncomfortable.
principles.shadow: The hunt for opportunity goes wrong when it becomes restless chasing: jumping at every scheme and sure thing while you neglect the work in front of you. It also goes wrong when it sees other people's trouble only as a chance to profit. Look closely, test small, and keep your dealings honest.

principles.title: First things first
principles.motto: Do the one thing that matters most, before anything else.
principles.essence: Your time and attention are limited, and most of what fills a day is not what builds a life. Decide what matters most, do it first, and learn to say no to the good things that crowd out the best.
principles.depth: Seneca warned his friend Lucilius in his second letter: nusquam est qui ubique est, the one who is everywhere is nowhere. Modern research agrees that scattered attention has a price. Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans (2001) measured the time lost each time people switch between tasks. Sophie Leroy (2009) studied attention residue: thoughts still stuck on an unfinished task. She found that it drags down performance on the next one. Bluma Zeigarnik's 1927 finding that unfinished tasks nag at memory has had mixed success in later repeat studies. But E. J. Masicampo and Roy Baumeister (2011) found that simply making a concrete plan for a task eased that nagging. That is one reason a written list calms the mind. Economics adds opportunity cost: the true price of any choice is the best thing you gave up to make it. Dwight Eisenhower, in a 1954 speech, quoted an unnamed college president who said the urgent problems are seldom the important ones. The so-called Eisenhower matrix grew from that line much later. Aristotle opened the Nicomachean Ethics with archers. Would we not hit the mark better, he asked, if we knew our chief aim, as archers know their target? In money, focus means fewer goals pursued fully. Clear one debt before the next, master one skill, and make one business work before you start another.

tales.title: Six Lines on a Sheet of Paper
tales.who: Ivy Lee, an adviser to business leaders, and Charles M. Schwab, president of Bethlehem Steel
tales.when: Early twentieth century (legend; often dated to about 1918)
tales.where: Bethlehem Steel, Pennsylvania
tales.source: A story retold in business books and speeches for many decades; no record from the time confirms the meeting or the payment
tales.tale:
A busy man sits behind a wide desk, and the papers on it are piled like snowdrifts: telegrams, letters, reports from the mills. Through the window, the steelworks breathe smoke into a grey Pennsylvania sky. The man is Charles M. Schwab, president of Bethlehem Steel, one of the richest and busiest men in America.

Across from him sits a quiet visitor, Ivy Lee, an adviser who would later be called one of the fathers of public relations. Both men were real. What follows is the story as it is told, again and again, in business books and speeches. It is best treated as a legend, because no one has found a record from the time that proves it happened this way.

Schwab, the story goes, says something like this: show me a way to get more of the right things done, and I will pay you whatever it is worth. Lee hands him a blank sheet of paper. Each evening, he says, write down the six most important things you must do tomorrow. Number them in order of their true importance. Tomorrow morning, start on number one, and stay with it until it is finished. Then number two. Do not touch the next until the one before is done. Whatever is left at day's end goes onto the next evening's list. Do this every working day. Have your managers do it too. Try it as long as you like, then send me a cheque for what you think it is worth.

Schwab tries it. Weeks pass. Then, the legend says, he sends Lee a cheque for twenty-five thousand dollars, a fortune in those days, and calls it the most profitable lesson he ever learned.

Did he really? We may never know. The sum and the year drift between tellings. But the method itself is real, and anyone can test it tonight with a pencil.

Its power is not in the paper. It is in the deciding. Most of us begin the day with whatever shouts loudest. Lee's list makes you choose, the night before, in quiet, what deserves your best hours. The rest can wait.

Six lines. One at a time. The steel, after all, was poured one ladle at a time.
tales.reveals: Whether or not the cheque was real, the method works because it forces a choice before the day's noise begins. Focus is less about working faster than about deciding, in advance, what deserves your best hours.

tales.title: The List of Things to Avoid
tales.who: Warren Buffett and his personal pilot, named in the retellings as Mike Flint
tales.where: Omaha, Nebraska (as told)
tales.source: Retold in blogs, books and talks and credited to the pilot's own account; a widely told but unconfirmed story
tales.tale:
Picture a small plane resting on a quiet airfield, its engine cooling, ticking softly in the heat. Inside, a pilot and his famous passenger are talking, not about wind or fuel, but about the pilot's life.

The passenger is Warren Buffett, the investor from Omaha, Nebraska, one of the richest people in the world and known for living simply. The pilot, named in most retellings as Mike Flint, is said to have flown him for years. What follows is a story told widely in books, blogs and talks. It may have a real root, but Buffett himself has never confirmed it, as far as anyone has shown. Hold it as a parable with a famous name attached.

As it is told, Buffett asks the pilot about his goals. Then he gives him a simple exercise. Write down the twenty-five things you most want to do in your career and your life over the next few years. The pilot writes them out: places to fly, skills to learn, plans for his family, small dreams and large ones.

Now, says Buffett, circle the five that matter most. Only five. The pilot struggles, crossing out, choosing again. At last five circles sit on the page. So you have two lists, says Buffett. The pilot nods. He plans to work hard on the top five, and to give the other twenty some time when he can, a little here, a little there. They are still good goals, after all.

No, says Buffett, in the story. The other twenty are your avoid-at-all-costs list. Give them no attention until the five are done. They are the dangerous ones, because you care about them just enough to be pulled away.

That last turn is what makes the tale worth telling. Bad ideas are easy to refuse. The real thieves of a life are the good ideas, the pleasant side roads, the projects that are almost important. They do not rob you all at once. They take an hour, then an evening, then a year.

Whether or not it happened on that airfield, the lesson holds. Choosing five is hard not because the others are worthless, but because they are not. A focused life is built mostly of gentle, firm refusals, spoken to things you love a little.
tales.reveals: The tale's sharp point is that the greatest threat to focus is not bad options but good ones. To reach what matters most, you must deliberately set aside things you genuinely want, at least for a season.

practice: Tonight, try Ivy Lee's method: write the six most important tasks for tomorrow in order, and finish number one before you open your messages.
Write your own twenty-five goals, circle five, and copy the other twenty onto a page titled Not Now. Read it whenever you feel pulled sideways.
Choose one money goal for the next three months, such as an emergency fund, one debt, or one skill. Send every spare peso toward that single aim.
Guard one hour a day for your most important work, with your phone in another room. Notice what you finish, and how little you missed.
principles.shadow: Focus turns harmful when it becomes tunnel vision. You chase one target so hard that you neglect your health, your family or your conscience. Or you refuse to change course when the facts change. Keep your chief aims few, but let love and honesty rank above them all.

principles.title: Keep a part of all you earn
principles.motto: Pay your future self first, before the world sends its bills.
principles.essence: Before any peso goes to the landlord, the shop or the lender, set a fixed part aside for your future self. Treat it as untouchable. At first the amount matters less than the habit: a part of every income, every time, kept on purpose.
principles.depth:
Money left to the end of the month is usually gone by the end of the month. Behavioural economists call one reason present bias: we weigh today's wants far more heavily than tomorrow's needs. David Laibson modelled this pattern as hyperbolic discounting (1997), a way of valuing what is near far above what comes later. Saving whatever is left over asks willpower to win every single day, and it rarely does. Paying yourself first turns the order around. The saving happens once, at the start, before temptation gets a vote.

Richard Thaler's idea of mental accounting (1985) explains why a separate pot works. We treat money differently depending on the label we give it, so a peso marked "future" is harder to spend than a loose peso in the wallet. Defaults, what happens when you do nothing, are powerful too. Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea (2001) studied a firm that enrolled workers in its retirement plan automatically. Participation leapt, simply because doing nothing now meant saving. Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow plan (2004) let workers commit future raises to savings. Their average saving rate rose from about 3.5 to about 13.6 percent over some forty months.

Aristotle taught in the Nicomachean Ethics that virtues are formed by habit, by doing. Keeping a part is less a sum than a character you build, one payday at a time.

tales.title: The Scribe Who Paid Everyone but Himself
tales.who: Arkad, a poor scribe, and Algamish, a moneylender (fictional characters created by George S. Clason)
tales.where: Babylon, as Clason imagined it
tales.source: George S. Clason, The Richest Man in Babylon (1926)
tales.tale:
The clay was still soft when the rich man leaned over the young scribe's shoulder and asked how long the work would take.

This is how George Clason tells the story of Arkad in The Richest Man in Babylon, a little book of parables first published in 1926. Clason was an American map maker who dressed his lessons in the robes of old Babylon. The people are invented, and he never pretended otherwise. But the lesson has outlived him by a century.

Arkad, the tale goes, was a poor scribe who carved laws into clay tablets for a few coins. One day a wealthy moneylender named Algamish ordered a copy of a law and wanted it in two days.
