He called his followers over. "Verily I say unto you," he said, "That this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury: For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living."

Think about that arithmetic. By the counting of coins, she gave almost nothing. By the counting of the heart, she gave more than anyone, because a gift is measured not only by its size but by what is left after it. The rich gave from the top of the pile. She gave the whole pile.

Readers have argued over this scene for two thousand years. Some see in it a picture of pure, trusting generosity. Others notice what comes just before it: Jesus warns against religious teachers who "devour widows' houses," and they read the story as a lament. To them it shows a poor woman giving her last coins to a system that should have been caring for her. Both readings can be true at once, and both are worth keeping.

For you, the lesson is not to empty your purse. It is that no one is too poor to give, and that a small gift, given with your whole heart, is not small at all.

Somewhere, a coin no bigger than a fingernail is still falling. And we are still listening for its sound.
tales.reveals: Generosity is measured by proportion and heart, not by size, so it is open to everyone, even the poor. The second reading adds a warning: giving should never be squeezed out of those who cannot afford it, and a just community protects them first.

practice: Choose a giving share you can keep up, even 1 to 5 percent of your income. Set it aside on payday, the same way you set aside savings.
Give one hour of skill this week: teach a cousin to budget, fix a neighbour's resume, or help at a barangay feeding program or church outreach.
Before giving to a cause, ask three questions: Is it real? Does it help people help themselves? Will I learn what my gift did?
Journal: when did someone's small gift change your life? Write their name, then thank them or pass the same kind of gift on to someone else.
principles.shadow: Generosity goes wrong when it becomes show, guilt or self-ruin. Think of giving to be seen, giving to people who exploit you, or giving away the emergency fund your family needs. Give from surplus and with judgment, and keep your own house standing so you can keep giving.

principles.title: Money is a river, not a pond
principles.motto: Money is trust in motion; let it flow toward what builds.
principles.essence: Money is less a thing than a shared agreement, a record of trust that does its work only when it moves between people. Wealth grows where money flows toward useful work, honest exchange and people you trust, and it goes stale where it is buried in fear. Save on purpose, but let your saved money keep working too, lent and invested where it builds something.
principles.depth: The word currency comes from the Latin currere, to run. In 1911 the economist Irving Fisher wrote the equation of exchange, MV = PT: money times velocity equals prices times trade. Velocity means how often each unit of money changes hands. The same peso spent at a sari-sari store becomes the owner's income, then the supplier's, then the farmer's. John Maynard Keynes, in his General Theory (1936), described the paradox of thrift. If everyone suddenly hoards at once, spending falls, incomes fall, and total saving may not rise at all. For one household, saving is wise. The danger is money that sits idle and fearful, under a mattress, earning nothing and helping no one. Money saved in a sound bank or cooperative, or invested, still circulates, because it is lent to people who build houses and businesses. Psychology adds the norm of reciprocity, named by the sociologist Alvin Gouldner (1960): we feel bound to return what we receive. That is why fair exchange builds relationships, and why trust is the hidden capital beneath every economy. Aristotle, in the Politics, separated managing a household from money-making for its own sake. He warned that coin pursued without limit forgets what it is for. Money is a means, and means are meant to move.

tales.title: The Stone at the Bottom of the Sea
tales.who: The people of Yap; William Henry Furness III; Captain David O'Keefe; Milton Friedman
tales.where: Yap, in the Caroline Islands of Micronesia, and the quarries of Palau
tales.source: William Henry Furness III, The Island of Stone Money (1910); Milton Friedman, "The Island of Stone Money" (1991)
tales.tale:
On the island of Yap, in the western Pacific, great stone wheels lean against houses and line the village paths. Some are as small as a plate. Some stand taller than a man, with a hole in the middle where a pole once went through, so that many shoulders could carry them. Moss grows on them. Children climb them. They are money.

The Yapese call them rai. The stone did not come from Yap at all. Men sailed hundreds of kilometres to the islands of Palau, cut the limestone with simple tools and brought it home on rafts and canoes across open sea. Some of those men never came home. Every stone carried that story, the danger and the labour and the voyage, and the story was part of its worth.

Now the strange and beautiful part. When a large rai changed owners, it often did not move. It stayed exactly where it stood. Everyone simply knew that it belonged to someone else now. The money lived in the shared memory of the village, the way the money in your bank account lives in a ledger, the bank's book of who owns what.

An American traveller, William Henry Furness III, stayed on Yap in the early 1900s. He was told of a family whose wealth was a stone no one alive had ever seen. Long ago, it was said, it sank in a storm on the way home from Palau. The crew swore it had been large and fine, and so the village agreed it still counted. A stone at the bottom of the sea bought things on land. Furness wrote this down as he heard it; it is a tale the islanders told, not something anyone could check.

He also told how the German rulers of the island once wanted the roads repaired and the chiefs ignored them. So officials painted black crosses on the finest stones, claiming them as a fine. The villages, suddenly poor, fixed the roads. The crosses were washed off, and the people were rich again.

Later an Irish American captain, David O'Keefe, brought rai to Yap by ship, cut with iron tools and in far greater numbers. Islanders often valued his stones less. Money that cost no struggle carried less trust.

In 1991 the economist Milton Friedman wrote about Yap and saw our own world in it: gold sitting in vaults, changing owners without moving. Money, he understood, is not the stone. It is the agreement between people about the stone.
tales.reveals: Money is a living agreement, a ledger of trust that works only while people keep believing in it and passing it along. Its value rests on shared memory and real effort, and whoever controls the record of who owns what holds great power over a community.

tales.title: The Necklaces That Never Stop
tales.who: The Trobriand Islanders and their Kula partners; Bronislaw Malinowski
tales.where: The Trobriand Islands and the surrounding Massim islands, Papua New Guinea
tales.source: Bronislaw Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922)
tales.tale:
Imagine a ring of islands scattered across the sea east of New Guinea, a circle hundreds of kilometres wide. Around that circle, for generations, carved canoes have sailed out with conch shells sounding, carrying treasures that no one means to keep.

A young Polish anthropologist, Bronislaw Malinowski, lived among the Trobriand Islanders between 1915 and 1918, while the First World War raged far away. He learned their language, sat by their fires and watched the great sea journeys he would describe in his book Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922). The islanders called the system Kula. He called it the Kula ring.

Two kinds of treasure travel the ring. Long necklaces of red shell discs, called soulava, move one way, clockwise around the islands. White armshells, called mwali, move the other way. When a man sails to his partner on a distant island, he may come home with a necklace. Months later, a partner from the opposite side arrives, and an armshell is given in return. Nobody hoards them. A famous piece may stay with you for a while, long enough for its name to be spoken with yours, and then it must go on.

Think how odd that is to a mind trained by the market. The treasures are not used to buy anything. You cannot eat them. Their worth lies in their history, the long line of hands that once held them, and in the honour of being, for a season, the one who passes them on. A great man in the Kula was not the one who kept the most. He was the one through whom the most had flowed.

Alongside the Kula, the islanders also bartered everyday goods, yams and pots and fish, and they drew a sharp line between that haggling and the dignity of the Kula gift. The ceremonial gifts built partnerships that could last a lifetime. Those bonds made trade safer, made the sea less lonely and made the next island a place where someone would welcome you by name.

Malinowski's account has been studied and questioned for a century, and the Kula has changed with the times, but it is still practised in the region today. Its quiet wisdom travels further than any canoe. In the end, what you are known for is not what you held. It is what moved through your hands, and where it went next.
tales.reveals: In the Kula, standing comes from passing wealth on, not from holding it, and the giving builds the trust that makes all other trade possible. Your money, too, gains meaning when it moves, strengthening the relationships and the community that hold you up.

practice: For one week, notice where your pesos go. How much stays near you (the carinderia, the sari-sari store, the local tailor), and how much flows far away? Move one regular purchase to a local seller you trust.

Check that your savings are working, not sleeping. Cash in a drawer earns nothing and can be lost or stolen. Money in a sound, insured bank, a well-run cooperative or a government savings program is lent onward to build things.
Pay what you owe on time, especially to small businesses and workers. Prompt payment is circulation: your bill paid on Friday is someone's groceries on Saturday.
Look around your home for things sitting idle. Sell, lend or give away three items someone else could use this month.
principles.shadow: Circulation becomes an excuse for overspending when "money must flow" turns into money flowing out faster than it comes in. Keep the reservoir full first, and let the river run from the overflow.

principles.title: What you thank grows
principles.motto: Count your blessings first, and every other count comes out truer.
principles.essence: Gratitude is the habit of noticing what you already have and who helped you get it. It will not make your bills smaller, but it changes the mind that pays them. Grateful people tend to feel richer, compare less and spend less trying to impress. They also keep the relationships that are real wealth. Without gratitude, no amount is ever enough.
principles.depth: Psychologists call the trap hedonic adaptation. A raise, a new phone or a bigger house delights you for a while, then becomes the new normal, and desire moves on. Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell named it the hedonic treadmill in 1971. Gratitude is one of the few known brakes. In 2003 Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough asked volunteers to write down, weekly or daily, things they were grateful for. Others listed hassles or simply events. The gratitude writers reported feeling better about their lives and more hopeful, and in one study slept better too. Later reviews, such as Davis and colleagues (2016), find the benefits real but small, and not always larger than other positive exercises. So treat gratitude as a steady habit, not a cure. It also protects against upward social comparison: measuring yourself against those above you. Leon Festinger described social comparison in 1954, and the upward kind feeds envy and debt. Seneca put the economics plainly in his second letter to Lucilius: "It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor." Cicero, in his speech For Plancius, called gratitude not only the greatest of the virtues but the parent of all the others. What you notice, you value; what you value, you tend; what you tend, grows.

tales.title: Five Small Lines a Week
tales.who: Robert Emmons, Michael McCullough and their volunteers
tales.where: United States
tales.source: Robert A. Emmons and Michael E. McCullough, "Counting Blessings Versus Burdens," Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (2003)
tales.tale:
A student sits at a desk at the end of a long week. The page in front of her has five empty lines. The instruction is simple, almost too simple: write down up to five things in your life you are grateful for. She chews her pen. Then she writes. My roommate made soup. My grandmother called. The sun came out on Thursday.

She stands for the volunteers in a study by two psychologists, Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough, published in 2003. In the first experiment, a group of university students was split three ways. Some were asked to list blessings. Others listed hassles: the parking, the bills, the friend who let them down. A third group simply wrote down events that had happened. Once a week, for ten weeks, they wrote.

Nothing else changed in their lives. Nobody was given money. Nobody got a new job. And yet, by the end, the gratitude writers felt better about their lives as a whole and more hopeful about the week ahead. They reported fewer aches and complaints, and said they spent more time exercising. Five small lines a week had tilted the way they saw everything else.

The researchers tried again with a harder group: adults living with neuromuscular diseases, illnesses that slowly steal strength from the body. Each evening for three weeks, some of them wrote down their blessings. They reported more good moods, more satisfaction with life and longer, better sleep. The people closest to them noticed a difference too.

Science should be honest about its limits, and so should we. Later reviews of many gratitude studies found the effects real but modest, sometimes no bigger than other kind exercises, like imagining your best possible future. Gratitude is not magic. It will not cure an illness or pay a debt.

But look at what it does. It turns the eye. A mind that hunts for what is missing will always find it, in a neighbour's new car, in a cousin's photos from abroad. A mind that has practised noticing soup, a phone call and a Thursday sun begins to feel what it already holds. And a person who feels rich is far less likely to borrow money in order to look rich.

The student closes her notebook. The bills on her desk have not changed. She has.
tales.reveals: Gratitude works by retraining attention, so that the abundance already in your life becomes visible. Its measured effects are modest but real, and a person who feels they have enough is far better protected against envy, comparison and debt.

tales.title: The Flounder and the Darkening Sea
tales.who: A poor fisherman, his wife Ilsebill and an enchanted flounder
tales.when: Folk tale; written down by the painter Philipp Otto Runge around 1806, published by the Brothers Grimm in 1812
tales.where: A hut by the sea, in Runge's telling the Baltic coast of Pomerania
tales.source: Brothers Grimm, Children's and Household Tales (1812), tale 19, "The Fisherman and His Wife," from Runge's Low German version
tales.tale:
There was once a fisherman who lived with his wife in a hut by the sea. It was a place so poor and dirty that the old German tellers called it a pot. Every day he went and sat on the rocks with his line, and every day the water was clear and bright.

One day he pulled up a great flounder, a flat fish, and the fish spoke. "Let me live," it said. "I am not really a fish. I am an enchanted prince." The fisherman, a gentle man, let it go, and it sank, leaving a long streak of blood in the water. He went home and told his wife.

"You asked for nothing?" said his wife, whose name was Ilsebill. "Go back and ask for a little cottage." So he went down to the shore and called the fish with a small rhyme, and the fish came. "Go home," it said. "She has it already." And there stood a cottage with a garden, hens and ducks, and a tidy kitchen. For a week or two, Ilsebill was content.

Then the cottage felt small. She wanted a stone castle, and got it. Then she wanted to be king, and she was king. Then emperor. Then pope. Each time, the fisherman walked to the sea with a heavier heart. And each time the water had changed: green and yellow, then grey and thick, then dark and foul-smelling, the wind rising, the sky the colour of a bruise.

On the last night she could not sleep. She watched the sun come up and was furious that she had not made it rise herself. "Go," she said. "Tell the fish I want to be like God." The fisherman went down into a storm so wild that houses and trees blew over and the waves rose as high as church towers. He shouted his rhyme into the wind.

"Go home," said the flounder. "She is sitting in her old pot again." And there they sat, and there, the tale says, they are sitting still.

Notice what was missing at every stage. Not money. Not power. Not land. What Ilsebill never had was a single day of thanks. Each gift became only the floor she stood on to reach for the next. A heart that cannot say "this is enough, and I am glad" will turn a palace back into a pot.
tales.reveals: This is the shadow of the principle. Without gratitude, every gain becomes the starting line for a new craving, and the craving can end by destroying what was gained. Abundance received without thanks never feels like abundance at all.

practice: Each evening this week, write three specific things you are grateful for. Include one about money (a paid bill, a fair price, a raise, a sale) and one about a person.
Write a gratitude letter to someone who helped you with money or taught you about it: a parent, a relative working abroad or a first boss. Read it to them if you can.
Before any non-essential purchase above an amount you set, pause and name something similar you already own and enjoy. Then decide.
When you catch yourself comparing (a classmate's car, a cousin's travel photos), name one thing you have that you would not trade. Mute accounts that leave you feeling poor.
principles.shadow: Gratitude goes wrong when it is used to excuse unfairness or silence real needs ("be thankful and don't ask for a fair wage"). Be thankful for what you have and still work, ask and negotiate for what you are owed.

principles.title: Build what outlives you
principles.motto: Spend your life on something that will outlast it.
principles.essence: Your legacy is what your wealth, work and character keep doing after you are gone. Decide early what you want your life to build: a family secure and educated, a skill handed on or a cause served. Let that purpose guide how you earn, keep and give. A legacy is not only for the rich. It is made in daily choices, and it is best begun while you are alive to watch it grow.
principles.depth: Erik Erikson, in Childhood and Society (1950), described a stage of adult life he called generativity versus stagnation. Generativity is the deep need, especially in middle age, to guide the next generation and create what will outlast you. The psychologist Dan McAdams and others later studied it. Adults who score high in generativity tend to report greater well-being and a stronger sense of meaning. Legacy thinking also corrects a common error of the mind: present bias, the habit of overvaluing today and discounting tomorrow. The economist David Laibson modelled it in 1997. Asking how you want to be remembered pulls the far future into the present, where it can shape today's choices. Kimberly Wade-Benzoni and colleagues (2012) found that people prompted to think about their legacy became more generous toward future generations. In On Old Age, Cicero quotes the poet Caecilius Statius: "Serit arbores, quae alteri saeclo prosint," he plants trees to benefit another generation. Practically, legacy also means plain paperwork: a written will, named beneficiaries, insurance where it is needed and honest family conversations. Beneficiaries are the people you name to receive an account or policy. Good paperwork means those you love are not left with confusion, quarrels or debt. A legacy is not a monument. It is a direction you choose while you still can.

tales.title: The Merchant of Death Is Dead
tales.who: Alfred Nobel; his brother Ludvig; Ragnar Sohlman
tales.where: Cannes, Paris and San Remo; Stockholm, Sweden
tales.source: Alfred Nobel's will (1895), published by the Nobel Foundation; biographies of Nobel. The obituary story is widely told, but the original newspaper article has not been found.
tales.tale:
Imagine opening a newspaper over breakfast and finding your own death in it. And worse: finding out what the world truly thinks of you.

That, as the story is told, is what happened to Alfred Nobel in 1888. His older brother Ludvig had died in Cannes, on the coast of France. A French newspaper, it is said, mixed up the two brothers and printed an obituary of Alfred instead. The headline read "Le marchand de la mort est mort": the merchant of death is dead. It said he had grown rich by finding ways to kill more people, faster, than ever before.

Here we must be careful. Ludvig did die in Cannes in 1888, and some reports did confuse him with Alfred. But historians have not found the article with that famous headline, and some doubt it was ever printed. The scene of Nobel reading it and being changed may be partly true, or a legend that survived because it fits so well.

What is certain is the life. Nobel was a Swedish chemist and inventor. In 1864 an explosion at the family's workshop in Stockholm killed his younger brother Emil and several others. Nobel went on to invent dynamite, patented in 1867, a safer way to handle the dangerous liquid nitroglycerine, and it blasted tunnels, mines and canals across the world. It was used in war too, and his companies made explosives and, later, arms. He became one of the richest men in Europe: restless, often lonely, never married.

On 27 November 1895, in Paris, he signed a handwritten will of four pages. He left most of his fortune, roughly 31 million Swedish kronor, to fund yearly prizes for those who had "conferred the greatest benefit to mankind" in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace. His friend Bertha von Suttner, a leading campaigner for peace, had long urged him toward that last cause. He died in San Remo the following year. His relatives were shocked and fought the will, and a young assistant, Ragnar Sohlman, spent years making it real. The first prizes were given in 1901.

Whether a newspaper woke him or his own conscience did, Nobel chose, near the end, what his name would mean. Today hardly anyone hears it and thinks first of dynamite. They think of the prize.
tales.reveals: A legacy is a choice you can still make, even late, even after a life you partly regret. The story also shows the power of imagining your own obituary. Seeing your life from its end can redirect what you do with the time and wealth you have left.

tales.title: The Billionaire with the Cheap Watch
tales.who: Charles "Chuck" Feeney
tales.where: New York, San Francisco, Ireland and around the world
tales.source: Conor O'Clery, The Billionaire Who Wasn't (2007); records of The Atlantic Philanthropies; news reports at his death in 2023
tales.tale:
On his wrist was a plastic watch that cost about fifteen dollars. He flew economy, carried his papers in a plastic bag and, in his last years, lived in a small rented apartment. People seated beside him on a plane never guessed that this quiet, rumpled man had once been a billionaire, and had given almost all of it away.

Charles Feeney, called Chuck, was born in 1931 in Elizabeth, New Jersey, to a working Irish American family, in the hard years of the Great Depression. He served in the US Air Force, went to Cornell University with the help of a veterans' scholarship and sold sandwiches in the dormitories at night to get by. In 1960 he and a partner, Robert Miller, founded Duty Free Shoppers, selling tax-free goods to travellers. It grew enormous.

By the early 1980s he was rich beyond any need, and he felt the weight of it. In 1982 he set up a foundation. In 1984 he quietly signed over almost his entire share of the business to it, keeping only a modest sum for himself and his family. He told almost no one. Those who received grants were asked not to reveal where the money came from. For years, hospitals, universities and peacemakers received gifts from a giver with no name.

The secret broke in 1997, when a business dispute over the sale of the company forced the facts into the open. The world learned that one of its most generous men had been hiding in plain sight. His foundation, The Atlantic Philanthropies, gave away about 8 billion dollars over his lifetime. It gave to universities across Ireland, north and south, to the peace process there, to health care in Vietnam and South Africa, and to research. And it gave to Cornell, the school that had once let a poor boy in.

Feeney had a name for his way: giving while living. Why wait until you die, he asked, when you can see the good your money does now? He also chose to close his foundation rather than let it run forever. In September 2020, its work done, Atlantic shut its doors, and Feeney signed the final papers in his small apartment.

He died in 2023, aged 92. He left no tower with his name on it. He left buildings that do not bear his name, programmes that outlived him and countless lives that never knew who helped them, which was exactly what he wanted.
tales.reveals: A legacy can be built quietly, while you are alive to guide it, without seeking credit. Feeney also shows that keeping your own life simple is what frees the surplus to do great good.

practice: Write your own short obituary, the one you hope will be true in forty years. Then list three things you could start this month to make it true.

Make or update a simple will. Check that beneficiaries (the people who will receive the money) are named on your accounts, insurance and SSS or other benefits. Tell your family where the papers are kept.
Teach one money skill to a younger person, such as a child, a niece or a new co-worker. Show them how to save, how compounding (returns earning their own returns) works or how to spot a scam.
Start one small thing meant to outlast you: a tree, a scholarship fund among cousins, a family recipe book or a habit of mentoring.
principles.shadow: Legacy turns into vanity when it is about your name on a building. It turns into control when you try to rule your heirs from the grave. Build for the good of others, and leave people free.

principles.title: Rise together
principles.motto: Wealth built with others outlasts wealth built against them.
principles.essence: The surest wealth is rarely built alone. Share gains with workers, partners and neighbours, and build groups where people own and decide together. Then trust grows, waste falls and the whole community grows sturdier, you included. Look for arrangements where both sides win, cooperate generously and keep the agreements clear.
principles.depth: Economists once assumed shared resources were doomed. Garrett Hardin's essay The Tragedy of the Commons (1968) argued that people will always overuse what no one owns. Elinor Ostrom spent decades studying fisheries, forests and irrigation systems, including the zanjera irrigation societies of Ilocos in the Philippines. In Governing the Commons (1990) she showed that communities often manage shared resources well for centuries. They do it when they set clear rules, watch fairly for cheating and make decisions together. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel prize in economics. Laboratory games point the same way. In public goods games, players choose how much to put into a common pot. Ernst Fehr and Simon Gachter (2002) found that cooperation collapses when free riders (people who take without putting in) go unchecked. It stays high when people can hold one another to account. Robert Putnam, in Bowling Alone (2000), called the trust and networks between people social capital. He linked it to safer streets, better health and better-run towns. Filipinos already have a word for this: bayanihan, neighbours lifting a house together. Aristotle wrote in the Politics that humans are by nature political animals, made to live in community. Cooperation is not charity. It lowers the cost of trust, spreads risk and lets many small people do what only the rich could do alone.

tales.title: The Mills by the Falls of Clyde
tales.who: Robert Owen and the mill families of New Lanark
tales.where: New Lanark, beside the River Clyde, Scotland
tales.source: Robert Owen, A New View of Society (1813 to 1816) and The Life of Robert Owen, Written by Himself (1857); histories of the New Lanark mills
tales.tale:
The River Clyde comes down through a deep green valley in Scotland, white with waterfalls, and beside it stand tall stone mills. Around 1800, the water turned great wheels there, and the wheels turned thousands of spindles. Among the spindles worked children, some only six or seven years old, many of them orphans sent from the poorhouses of Glasgow and Edinburgh.

In 1799 a young Welsh manager named Robert Owen, the son of a saddler, bought the mills with partners from David Dale, whose daughter Caroline he had just married. He took charge on the first day of 1800. Owen believed something radical for his time: that people are shaped by the conditions they live in, and that if you improve the conditions, you improve the people.

So he began to change them. He stopped taking young children into the mills and shortened the working day. He opened a village store that sold good food and goods close to cost, instead of the overpriced company shops common elsewhere. He cleaned the streets and improved the houses. In 1816 he opened the Institute for the Formation of Character, with what is often called the first infant school in Britain. There small children learned through play, music and dancing instead of the cane.

Around 1806, a quarrel between Britain and the United States cut off the supply of cotton, and the mills fell silent. Owen later wrote that he kept paying his workers their full wages for four months, at a cost of about 7,000 pounds. People remembered that. Trust earned in a crisis does not leave easily.

And the mills made money. That surprised his partners, some of whom wanted more profit and less schooling. Owen bought them out with new partners, among them the philosopher Jeremy Bentham, who agreed to take a modest return of about five percent. Thousands of visitors came to see the experiment for themselves, including the young Grand Duke Nicholas, later Tsar of Russia.

Not all of Owen's dreams came true. His model community at New Harmony, Indiana, founded in 1825, fell apart within a few years, and some of his workers found him a kind but controlling master. But the mills still stand, now a World Heritage Site. The idea he tested there, that a business can prosper by lifting the people inside it, has never gone away.
tales.reveals: Sharing gains with workers can make a business more stable and trusted, not weaker, when it is run soundly. Owen's failures are part of the lesson: shared prosperity needs good systems and real participation, not only a generous founder.

tales.title: The Priest and the Five Students
tales.who: Father Jose Maria Arizmendiarrieta and five of his former students
tales.when: 1941 to today (the first cooperative, ULGOR, founded 1956)
tales.where: Mondragon (Arrasate), in the Basque Country of northern Spain
tales.source: William Foote Whyte and Kathleen King Whyte, Making Mondragon (1988); histories published by the Mondragon Corporation
tales.tale:
In 1941 a young priest arrived in Mondragon, a small industrial town in a narrow Basque valley in northern Spain. The civil war had just ended. The town was poor, hungry and bitterly divided, and the good jobs in its factories went mostly to those with connections. The priest, Jose Maria Arizmendiarrieta, had worked as a journalist for the Basque side in the war and had been captured, and he had come close to being shot.

He did not preach much about heaven. He talked about work and about learning. In 1943 he opened a small technical school for local boys, paid for by families in the town. He taught that work gives a person dignity, and that ordinary workers could own and run their own businesses if they were trained, organised and willing to cooperate.

In 1956 five of his former students did exactly that. With their savings, loans from friends and neighbours, and a licence to build paraffin stoves, they started a workshop called ULGOR. The name was made from the first letters of their surnames. Every worker was an owner. Every owner had one vote, however much money he had put in. Pay was kept close together: at first, the best paid earned no more than about three times the lowest.

In 1959, urged on by the priest, they founded a cooperative bank, the Caja Laboral. Now the savings of working families could fund new cooperatives instead of flowing away to distant investors. The bank helped start dozens more. From one workshop grew a family of cooperatives making appliances, machine tools and car parts, with schools, a university and a chain of shops.

Today the Mondragon group employs roughly 70,000 people by its own recent counts. Its pay gaps are still far narrower than in most companies, though wider than in the early days. It has known loss. In 2013 Fagor, the appliance maker that grew from that first stove workshop, collapsed in Spain's debt crisis. Many of its members were moved into other cooperatives, but not all, and critics point out that many workers in its factories abroad are not owners at all.

Arizmendiarrieta died in 1976. He never grew rich. Yet in that valley, where a priest once taught hungry boys to use their hands and their votes, the machines still hum. Many of them belong to the people who run them.
tales.reveals: When people own and govern together, they can build wealth that stays in the community and lasts for generations. Mondragon also shows the limits: cooperatives still face markets, debt and failure, and their ideals need constant tending.

practice: Join or start a paluwagan (a rotating savings circle), cooperative or savings group only with clear written rules. Agree who pays, how much, when, what happens if someone misses, and who keeps the records.
If you run a business or lead a team, share one gain this month. It could be a small profit share, a bonus tied to team results or a real voice in a decision that affects them.
Practise bayanihan: offer your skill to a neighbour's project this week, and accept help when it is offered to you.
Journal: who has helped you rise, and whom are you helping rise? List names on both sides and notice where the list is thin.
principles.shadow: Shared ventures fail when trust is blind: unwritten rules, no records, a charming leader nobody checks, or friends pooling money they cannot afford to lose. Cooperate generously, but keep clear agreements and open books.

principles.title: Health is the first wealth
principles.motto: Guard the body that carries every other treasure you will ever hold.
principles.essence: Your body is the account every other account is drawn from. Money can buy care, but it cannot buy back years spent carelessly. So tend your health first: plain food, daily movement, sleep and friends, long before illness sends the bill.
principles.depth: Economists treat health as a form of capital. Michael Grossman's 1972 model described it as a stock, a store you are born with. It wears down with age, and you can add to it through food, rest, exercise and care. Every working day you will ever have is drawn from it. Behavioural science explains why we neglect it. Present bias is the pull of a small reward now over a larger one later (studied by David Laibson and others). It makes the cake tonight feel more real than your heart at sixty. Daniel Kahneman's "focusing illusion" shows that we overrate how much one change, like a raise, will alter our lives. We also underrate the quiet goods we already have. Large, long-running studies keep pointing to the same few habits: not smoking, regular movement, a diet rich in plants, a healthy weight, little alcohol, enough sleep. The ancients saw the pattern. Seneca observed that people who guard their property closely are careless with their lives. Solon, in Herodotus, counted a sound body and freedom from sickness among the marks of a fortunate person. Be honest about the limits: genes, accidents and poverty shape health too, and no habit is a guarantee. But habits shift the odds, and odds kept for decades become a life.

tales.title: Eight Parts Full
tales.who: The elders of Okinawa; Dr Makoto Suzuki of the Okinawa Centenarian Study
tales.where: Okinawa, Japan
tales.source: Okinawa Centenarian Study (begun by Makoto Suzuki, 1975); Bradley Willcox, Craig Willcox and Makoto Suzuki, The Okinawa Program (2001); Japanese prefectural life expectancy tables (2000)
tales.tale:
Picture a bowl of purple sweet potato steaming on a low table. An old woman lifts her chopsticks, pauses, and says three words before she eats: hara hachi bu. Eat until your belly is eight parts full, out of ten. Then stop, while you could still eat more.

On the islands of Okinawa, in the far south of Japan, people have said these words at meals for generations. Some trace the saying to old Confucian teaching. It asks for very little. Not a fast, not a feast. Only a small space left empty at the end of every meal, like a cup not filled to the brim.

In 1975 a young doctor named Makoto Suzuki began to visit the island's oldest people. He checked their records, listened to their hearts and asked about their days. He found what the world would later make famous: for its size, Okinawa had more people past one hundred than almost anywhere he could measure. Their hearts were strong. They ate vegetables, tofu, seaweed and sweet potato, with little meat. They tended gardens into their nineties. Many belonged to a moai, a circle of friends who met for life and carried each other through hard times.

Then the story turned, and the turning is part of the lesson. After the war, American bases came to the islands, and with them burgers, canned meat and cars. The young ate the new way and walked less. By 2000, Okinawan men had fallen from near the top of Japan's life expectancy tables to twenty-sixth of its forty-seven prefectures. The islanders called it the 26 shock. The elders were still old and well. Their grandchildren were not following them.

Honesty asks one more thing of the listener. Some researchers doubt the oldest birth records around the world, and many Okinawan papers burned in the war, so a few of the greatest ages may be uncertain. No one has shown the whole picture to be false. But a wise listener holds the numbers lightly.

What remains is simpler than any number. A long life was not bought there. It was gathered, meal by meal, walk by walk, friend by friend, in amounts so small that no one noticed them being saved.

The old woman sets down her chopsticks. There is still potato in the bowl. She is not hungry, and she is not full. She is exactly where a long life begins.
tales.reveals: Health is built the way wealth is: by small, repeated deposits that look like nothing on any single day. Okinawa also shows the reverse, that a single generation of new habits can spend down an inheritance of long lives.

tales.title: Call No One Happy Until the End
tales.who: Croesus, king of Lydia; Solon, lawgiver of Athens; Cyrus, king of Persia
tales.when: 6th century BC, as Herodotus told it c. 430 BC
tales.where: Sardis, capital of Lydia (in today's western Turkey)
tales.source: Herodotus, Histories, Book 1 (chapters 30 to 33 and 85 to 87); the meeting itself is doubted by historians
tales.tale:
Gold lay in heaps in the treasure rooms of Sardis, so much of it that every lamp seemed to burn twice. Croesus, king of Lydia, walked his guest through room after room. The guest was Solon, the lawgiver of Athens, a man famous for wisdom, and Croesus wanted that wisdom to say one thing.

When the tour was over, the king asked his question. Of all the people you have seen in your travels, who is the happiest?

Tellus of Athens, said Solon. Croesus waited. Tellus, Solon explained, lived in a good city in good times. He had fine sons, he saw each of them have children, and all of them lived. He died fighting for his city and was buried with honour where he fell.

Croesus, stung, asked who came second. Surely now. Solon named two brothers of Argos, Cleobis and Biton, strong young men. On a feast day, when the oxen were late, they put themselves under the yoke and pulled their mother's cart for miles to the temple of Hera. Their mother prayed that the goddess give her sons the best thing a person can have. That night they lay down in the temple, and they did not wake.

Now the king was angry. Is my happiness worth nothing? Solon spoke gently. A very rich man is not luckier than one who has enough for each day, he said, unless his luck holds to the end. The fortunate one is whole in body, free from sickness and trouble, glad in his children. So wait. Until a life is finished, call it fortunate, not yet happy.

Croesus sent him away as a fool. Then the years arrived. His beloved son was killed by accident in a boar hunt. He made war on Persia, trusting an oracle he had misread, and lost his kingdom. Cyrus, the Persian king, set him on a great pile of wood to burn. On the pyre, Herodotus says, Croesus groaned one name three times: Solon. Cyrus asked what it meant, heard the story, and thought of his own fortune. As the tale is told, rain fell from a clear sky and put out the flames.

Historians doubt that the two men ever met, since Solon's travels seem to come too early for Croesus's reign. Herodotus was telling a truth, not keeping a diary. And the truth was this: the gold was in the rooms, but the happiness was in the body, the children and the ending.
tales.reveals: Croesus measured his life by what he held; Solon measured it by health, family and how it ends. Wealth can be lost in an afternoon. So the wise invest early in goods that money cannot guard: a sound body and the people who love you.

practice: Eat one meal a day this week at hara hachi bu. Stop when you feel about eight parts full out of ten, wait ten minutes, and notice whether you still want more.
Walk for thirty minutes on at least five days. The walk to the market or the jeepney stop counts; the habit matters more than the speed.
Book the check-up you have been putting off (blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol), and ask what your PhilHealth membership or local health centre already covers.
Journal on Solon's question: if your life is to end well, what will your body need from you over the next ten years? Write one habit to start and one to stop.
principles.shadow: Health can become an idol of its own: anxious tracking, costly supplements and quiet blame for people who fall ill through no fault of theirs. Care for your body as a steward, not a judge, and remember that illness is often luck, not failure.

principles.title: Rich in time
principles.motto: Money is renewable. Your hours are not. Spend them like the rarer coin.
principles.essence: Time is the one currency you cannot earn more of, and the only one you spend whether you choose to or not. To be wealthy, in the end, is to own your hours. It means enough freedom to spend them on what matters to you, now and not only in some far-off retirement.
principles.depth: Seneca opened On the Shortness of Life (c. AD 49) with a reversal. Life is not short, he said; we make it short by wasting it. People who would never let a stranger take their money hand their hours to anyone who asks. Henry David Thoreau sharpened the point in Walden (1854): "the cost of a thing is the amount of what I will call life which is required to be exchanged for it, immediately or in the long run." Economists call this opportunity cost: the true price of anything is what you give up to get it. We are poor at counting it because money is visible and time is not. We cross the city to save fifty pesos and never price the afternoon. Ashley Whillans and colleagues describe "time poverty", the chronic sense of having too much to do and too little time. They link it to lower well-being, even among people with good incomes. Cassie Mogilner (2010) found that merely thinking about time, rather than money, nudged people toward spending hours with others. For a family struggling to eat, more money is the urgent need. But once the basics are secure, guarding your hours is often the cheapest raise you will ever get.

tales.title: The Fisherman Who Was Already There
tales.who: A poor fisherman and a well-dressed tourist, in Heinrich Böll's story; in later retellings, a fisherman and a banker
tales.where: A harbour on the west coast of Europe (in later retellings, a village in Mexico)
tales.source: Heinrich Böll, "Anekdote zur Senkung der Arbeitsmoral" (Anecdote Concerning the Lowering of Productivity), 1963; later anonymous retellings. Retold here in original words.
tales.tale:
A small boat rocks against the harbour wall. Its owner lies in it with his cap over his eyes, half asleep, the morning catch already in a basket at his feet. The sun is warm. The water slaps the wood softly, like a hand patting a sleeping child.

Then a click. A tourist in smart clothes is taking pictures. Click, and again, click. The fisherman sits up. The tourist, a little embarrassed, offers him a cigarette, and they begin to talk.

Why are you not out at sea, the tourist asks. The weather is perfect. The fisherman says he has already been out. He caught enough. Enough for today, and for tomorrow, and a little more.

The tourist cannot bear it. He leans in, eager, kind in his way. Just think, he says. Go out three, four times a day. In a year you buy a motor. In two years, a second boat. Then a small fleet. A cold store, a smokehouse, a factory. A helicopter to spot the fish, a restaurant of your own, trucks to carry your catch to faraway cities. And then? asks the fisherman. And then, says the tourist, his eyes shining, you could sit here in the harbour, doze in the sun, and look at the beautiful sea.

The fisherman shrugs. But that is what I was doing, he says, before you started clicking.

The German writer Heinrich Böll wrote this little story in 1963, reportedly for a radio programme on the first of May, the workers' holiday. In his version the tourist walks away thoughtful, no longer pitying the poorly dressed fisherman, only a little envious of him. In the years since, the tale has passed from hand to hand and changed in the passing. The harbour became a Mexican village, the tourist became an American banker with a business degree, and the dream became selling the company for millions. Many who tell it have never heard of Böll.

The story is not a law of economics. The fisherman owns his boat and already has enough; many people do not, and for them the extra trip to sea means rice and school fees, not greed. But the question it asks belongs to everyone. What is all the work for? If the answer is rest, and time, and the sea, then look around before you set out. Some of it may already be yours.
tales.reveals: Many plans for wealth are secretly plans to buy back time, and some of that time is already within reach. The tale warns against endless postponement: the life you mean to enjoy later can quietly become the life you never had.

tales.title: Forty Dollars on a Saturday
tales.who: Ashley Whillans, Elizabeth Dunn, Paul Smeets, Rene Bekkers and Michael Norton
tales.where: Vancouver, Canada, with surveys in the United States, Canada, Denmark and the Netherlands
tales.source: Whillans, Dunn, Smeets, Bekkers and Norton, "Buying time promotes happiness", Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2017)
tales.tale:
A Saturday morning in Vancouver. A woman stands in her kitchen holding forty dollars that are not quite hers. A university experiment has given them to her, with one rule: spend it on something that will save you time.

She could pay a neighbour's teenager to mow the lawn. She could have dinner delivered. She could hire someone to clean the bathroom she has been avoiding for two weeks. She chooses one, and then, for an hour or two, she does something else with the time she bought.

She is imagined here, but the experiment was real. In 2017 a young researcher named Ashley Whillans published a study with a plain title: Buying time promotes happiness. She worked with Elizabeth Dunn in Vancouver and with colleagues in the United States and the Netherlands. Sixty working adults took part in the field test. On one weekend each was given forty dollars to spend on something that saved time. On another weekend, forty dollars to spend on a thing: clothes, a book, a bottle of wine. Each evening they reported how they felt.

After the time-saving weekend, people felt better. Not wildly, not forever, but clearly: more good feeling, less stress about the day.

The team also surveyed more than six thousand people in four countries, from ordinary earners to a group of Dutch millionaires. Those who spent money to free up time tended to be more satisfied with their lives, and the link held across incomes. Yet when the researchers asked people how they would spend an unexpected forty dollars, only a tiny few thought of buying time at all. Most chose things.

Science asks for care here. The survey shows a link, not a proof. The effects were modest, as most effects in psychology are, and one study is a beginning, not a final word. Buying time also needs spare money, which many families do not have. For them, time is freed in other ways: shared chores, bayanihan between neighbours, the courage to say no.

But the finding points at a quiet mistake most of us make. We count pesos with care. We hardly count hours. We will spend an afternoon to save a few coins, then wonder why we feel poor. The woman in the kitchen did not get richer that Saturday. She got her afternoon back, and it felt like wealth.
tales.reveals: Time is a form of wealth that money can sometimes buy back, yet we rarely think to do it. Once your needs are covered, the next peso may do more good buying an hour than buying a thing.

practice: For one week, note how you spend your hours in rough blocks. At the end, mark the hours you would buy back if you could, and the hours you would never sell.
Work out your true hourly wage: take-home pay divided by all the hours work really takes, including the commute and the recovery. Then price your next purchase in hours of life, as Thoreau suggested.
Make one small time trade this week: pay for a task you dread, share cooking with a neighbour, or swap childminding with a friend. Notice how you use the hour it frees.
Ask Böll's question in your journal: what is all this work for? Then name one part of the answer you could enjoy this month, not in thirty years.
principles.shadow: Guarding your time can slide into idleness, and selling all of it for money can become a life never lived. Work hard in the seasons that need it, but do not postpone every joy to a future that is not promised.

principles.title: Wealth is people
principles.motto: Count your wealth by who would come if you called at midnight.
principles.essence: The richest asset you can build is a web of warm, trusted relationships: family, friends, neighbours, colleagues. They keep you healthier and happier than money does, and they cannot be bought in a hurry, only grown over years of attention.
principles.depth: In 2010 Julianne Holt-Lunstad, Timothy Smith and Bradley Layton combined 148 studies covering more than 300,000 people. Those with stronger social ties had about 50 percent higher odds of surviving the years each study followed. The researchers compared the effect to that of quitting smoking. The figure is an average across very different studies. Cause can also run both ways, since healthy people find it easier to keep friends. But the broad finding has held. Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary argued in 1995 that the "need to belong" is a basic human drive, close to hunger in its force. Aristotle gave two of the ten books of his Nicomachean Ethics to friendship. He wrote that without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods. Economists speak of social capital: the trust and networks between people. Robert Putnam's Bowling Alone (2000) traced how they make communities safer and more prosperous. Filipino culture already holds a version of this in kapwa, the shared self that sees others as part of you. Relationships behave like other capital. They grow with steady deposits of time and attention, they decay when neglected, and they repay most when planted long before you need them.

tales.title: Seven Hundred Lives, One Lesson
tales.who: The men of the Grant Study and the Glueck Study; researchers Arlie Bock, George Vaillant and Robert Waldinger
tales.where: Cambridge and Boston, Massachusetts, USA
tales.source: Harvard Study of Adult Development; George Vaillant, Triumphs of Experience (2012); Robert Waldinger's public talk (2015) and published papers
tales.tale:
In the autumn of 1938, a group of Harvard students sat down for tests that would follow them for the rest of their lives. Doctors measured their bodies and listened to their hearts. Psychologists asked about their hopes and their fathers. They were bright young men, chosen because they seemed likely to do well. One of them, it later came out, was John F. Kennedy.

Across the river, in the poorer streets of Boston, another group was being studied: boys from crowded tenements, many from immigrant families who had arrived with almost nothing. Researchers named Sheldon and Eleanor Glueck had chosen them for a study of why some boys stayed out of trouble. In time the two studies were joined. Together they held about seven hundred and twenty-four lives.

Then the researchers did something rare. They kept going. Every two years a questionnaire arrived. Every few years came medical records, blood tests, and later brain scans, and interviews in the men's own living rooms. The young men became soldiers, lawyers, factory workers, drinkers, a president. Some grew rich. Some died young. The study outlived several of its leaders. George Vaillant directed it for more than thirty years, and the psychiatrist Robert Waldinger took it up after him.

When they laid the decades side by side, the answer surprised even them. It was not cholesterol at fifty that best predicted who would be healthy at eighty. It was how satisfied the men were with their relationships at fifty. The men with warm marriages and close friends, people they could call in the night, tended to live longer and keep their minds sharper. Lonely men declined sooner. Money and fame, chased so hard, mattered far less than anyone had guessed.

Waldinger said it plainly to a large audience in 2015: good relationships keep us happier and healthier. Not the number of friends. The warmth of them.

A careful listener should note the limits. The first men were all white and all male, so other studies, of women and of other peoples, were needed to confirm the findings. Many have since pointed the same way. The study shows strong links, not perfect proof of cause. Today it follows the men's children, more than a thousand of them.

Picture one old man near the end, the researcher's notebook open on his knee. He is not asked about his bank balance. He is asked who visits. And that, it turned out, was the whole question all along.
tales.reveals: Over a lifetime, the quality of your relationships may matter more to your health and happiness than your income. Time spent on people is not a cost to your wealth but one of its best investments.

tales.title: The Richest Woman and the Boy's Knee
tales.who: Hetty Green, financier, and her son Ned Green
tales.where: New Bedford, Massachusetts; Hoboken, New Jersey; New York City
tales.source: Newspaper accounts of her life and death (1890s to 1916); Charles Slack, Hetty (2004), and earlier biographies. The story of Ned's leg is disputed.
tales.tale:
A black dress, worn so long that its black has gone greenish at the seams. A woman walks to a bank in lower Manhattan in it, carrying a bag of papers. So the stories go, she sits on the floor of the vault to read them rather than pay rent for a desk. She is, by most counts, the richest woman in America.

Hetty Green was born in 1834 in New Bedford, Massachusetts, a whaling town that smelled of oil and salt. Her family's money came from ships. As a little girl she read the money pages of the newspaper aloud to her grandfather. She learned early what she would believe all her life: buy when others are afraid, keep cash, waste nothing.

She was brilliant. She bought railway and government bonds when others fled them. When panic struck New York in 1907, the city itself came to her for a loan. Newspapers called her the Witch of Wall Street. At her death in 1916 her fortune was reckoned at between one and two hundred million dollars, worth billions today. She also lived in cheap rented rooms in Hoboken, moving often, partly to dodge taxes. She haggled over pennies with grocers. And there is the story of her son's knee.

Ned Green hurt his knee as a boy, in a sledding accident, and it did not heal. As the story is usually told, his mother dressed them both in old clothes and took him to free clinics for the poor, to avoid a doctor's bill. When she was recognised and asked to pay, she left. The knee grew worse. Years later, as a young man, Ned lost the leg.

How much of this is true is still argued. Some later writers say she did spend money on doctors for Ned, and that the full story is more tangled than the legend. Newspapers loved to mock a rich, odd woman, and the tale grew in their hands. Perhaps she was frightened, and thrift had become the only way she knew to show care.

But the tale has lasted for a reason. People saw in it something true about money held too tightly: it can stand between you and the very people it was meant to protect. Ned later spent his share freely, on yachts and rare stamps, as if answering her.

A fortune of a hundred million dollars, and the thing everyone remembers is one boy, and one knee.
tales.reveals: Money is a tool for caring for people. Once it is guarded so fiercely that it cannot be spent on them, it has lost its purpose. Even if some details are legend, the tale endures because the danger it names is real.

practice: List the five to ten people who matter most to you. Beside each, write when you last spent real time together, then plan one visit, call or meal this week.
Join or revive a circle that meets regularly: a barkada lunch, a church group, a sports team, a paluwagan. Okinawans call a lifelong circle like this a moai; faithfulness matters more than size.
Give one hour of undivided attention each day this week: a meal or a conversation with your phone out of sight.
Journal on the Harvard question: who would you call at three in the morning in a crisis, and who would call you? If the list is short, choose one friendship to water.
principles.shadow: Treating people as contacts to use, or trying to buy affection with gifts, turns relationships into transactions and spoils them. Love people for themselves, and let money serve those bonds, never replace them or stand in their way.

principles.title: More is not always more
principles.motto: Enough is a finish line you draw yourself, or never reach at all.
principles.essence: Once your needs are met and your future is secure, more money brings smaller and smaller gains. Chasing it can cost you the things that matter more. Decide what enough looks like for you, in numbers and in a way of life, and let that line set you free.
principles.depth: Economists call it diminishing marginal utility: each extra unit of something adds less than the one before. The first bowl of rice when you are hungry means everything; the fifth means little. Daniel Bernoulli proposed in 1738 that the value of extra money depends on how much you already have. That is why income and happiness research usually works with doublings rather than pesos. The psychologists Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell (1971) named the "hedonic treadmill". We adapt to every gain and soon want more, so the finish line keeps moving away. Richard Easterlin (1974) found that as nations grew richer, average happiness rose less than expected, a finding still debated. Social comparison makes it worse, because we measure our wealth against our neighbours rather than our needs. The philosophers knew this. Epicurus taught that the wealth nature asks for is limited and easy to find, while the wealth of empty desire has no end. The Stoics practised simple living so that desire would loosen its grip. The writer of Proverbs prayed, "give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me" (Proverbs 30:8, King James Version). Enough is not poverty praised, and it is not a fixed sum: it depends on your family, your city and your risks. It is a decision, and once made, it frees your energy for everything else.

tales.title: The King Who Could Not Eat Gold
tales.who: King Midas of Phrygia; Silenus; the wine god Bacchus (Dionysus)
tales.when: Myth, as told by Ovid (c. AD 8)
tales.where: Phrygia (in today's Turkey) and the river Pactolus near Sardis
tales.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book XI; the daughter turned to gold was added by Nathaniel Hawthorne in A Wonder-Book (1852)
tales.tale:
A twig snaps in the king's hand, and before it falls it is gold. He laughs. He picks up a stone, and it gleams. He touches a clod of earth, and it becomes a heavy lump of treasure. He pulls an ear of wheat and holds a golden harvest. He plucks an apple, and it shines like fruit from the garden of the gods.

This is how the Roman poet Ovid tells it, in the eleventh book of his Metamorphoses, the long poem of changes. Midas was king of Phrygia. One day farmers found old Silenus, the drunken teacher of the wine god Bacchus, wandering lost in the hills, and led him to the palace bound in garlands. Midas knew him, feasted him for days, and returned him safely to his master. Bacchus was grateful. Choose any gift, he said. Midas did not pause. Let whatever I touch become gold.

The god granted it, sorry that the king had not asked for something better. And for one bright afternoon Midas was the richest man in the world. Water poured over his hands fell as a rain of gold. Doors turned to gold as he pushed them open.

Then his servants set a table before him. He reached for bread, and it hardened in his fingers. He lifted meat to his lips, and his teeth closed on metal. He drank wine mixed with water, and molten gold ran into his mouth. Rich and wretched, Ovid says, he longed to escape his wealth and hated what he had prayed for. Hunger sat with him at the golden table. Thirst burned in his throat.

He lifted his shining arms to the sky and begged forgiveness. Bacchus, kind that day, told him to go to the river Pactolus, near Sardis, and wash at its source. Midas plunged in. The gift left him and passed into the water, and the river's sands, the story says, have glittered with gold ever since.

You may remember a daughter, turned into a golden statue by her father's embrace. She is not in Ovid. The American writer Nathaniel Hawthorne added her in 1852, and she has stayed because she makes the cost impossible to miss.

Ovid tells us one more thing. After the river, Midas hated riches and went to live in the woods and fields. He had learned, at the price of one terrible meal, that gold is worth only what it can become: bread, water, and the touch of someone you love.
tales.reveals: Money is valuable only as a means to living, and wanting it without limit can cut you off from life itself. Midas held more gold than anyone, and it was the first moment in his story when he did not have enough.

tales.title: The Line That Moved
tales.who: Daniel Kahneman, Angus Deaton, Matthew Killingsworth and Barbara Mellers
tales.where: Princeton, New Jersey, and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA
tales.source: Kahneman and Deaton, PNAS (2010); Killingsworth, PNAS (2021); Killingsworth, Kahneman and Mellers, PNAS (2023)
tales.tale:
A phone buzzes in a pocket. A question lights the screen: How do you feel right now? A woman on a train taps her answer, then goes back to the window. All across America, over and over, tens of thousands of people answer that small question at random moments of their days.

But begin earlier, in 2010, at Princeton. Two scholars who would both win the Nobel prize, the psychologist Daniel Kahneman and the economist Angus Deaton, studied about 450,000 answers to a daily Gallup survey of Americans. They looked at two different things. First, how do people judge their life as a whole? That kept climbing as income rose, with no top in sight. Second, how do people feel from day to day: joy, worry, sadness? That rose too, and then, around 75,000 dollars a year, it seemed to flatten. Past that point, more money did not seem to make ordinary days feel better.

The 75,000 dollar line travelled the world. People quoted it at dinner. One American company even raised its lowest salaries toward it.

Then a young researcher named Matthew Killingsworth looked again, using a phone app he had built, with 1.7 million moments from more than 33,000 working Americans. In 2021 he reported that good feeling kept rising with income, with no plateau at all. The two findings clashed.

What happened next is rare in science. Instead of arguing in print for years, Kahneman and Killingsworth sat down together, with the psychologist Barbara Mellers as a fair referee, and went through the data side by side. This is called an adversarial collaboration: rivals working as partners. In 2023 they published what they found. For most people, happiness keeps rising with income. But for the unhappiest fifth, more income helps up to about 100,000 dollars a year, and then stops helping. Their sorrows, the authors suggested, are ones money cannot reach.

One more finding ran under all of it. The rise follows doublings, not dollars. Going from 20,000 to 40,000 lifts feeling about as much as going from 100,000 to 200,000. Each new step needs twice the money of the last.

These numbers are American, and costs in Manila or Cebu are different. But the shape travels. Money helps enormously when it lifts you out of want. After that it helps more slowly, and at some point the extra hours cost more than they bring. Enough is the place where you notice, and look out the window.
tales.reveals: More money brings real gains, above all out of poverty, but each extra gain costs more than the last, and some sorrows money cannot touch. Knowing this helps you judge when more income is worth the hours and when it is time to say enough.

practice: Write your "enough number": the monthly income and savings that would cover your needs, your emergency fund and your retirement plan. Beside it, write what you would do with your energy once you reach it.
Before your next large purchase, wait seven days and ask whether it meets a natural need or an empty desire, in Epicurus's sense.
Catch one comparison this week (a neighbour's car, a friend's posts) and name it to yourself: that is their line, not mine.
Try one simple day this month: plain meals, no shopping, a walk instead of paid entertainment. Notice how much of your comfort survives.
principles.shadow: The idea of enough can be used to excuse other people's poverty, or to give up on building the security you truly need. Draw your line honestly, high enough to protect your family and your future, and then help others reach theirs.

principles.title: Abundance is a way of living
principles.motto: Live open-handed: plant, share, travel light, and the world feels full.
principles.essence: Abundance is not a pile you reach one day but a way of moving through the world. It means planting more than you will harvest, giving freely from what you have, and holding things lightly and people closely. Build a secure base, but know that the feeling of plenty comes from how you live, not from how much you keep.
principles.depth: Sendhil Mullainathan and Eldar Shafir describe how scarcity narrows attention to what is missing (Scarcity, 2013). Barbara Fredrickson's broaden and build theory (1998, 2001) proposes the opposite movement. Positive emotions such as gratitude, joy and interest widen what we notice. Over time, they build lasting resources like friendships and skills. Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton (Science, 2008) found that spending money on others lifted happiness more than spending it on oneself. Aknin's later work found similar patterns in many countries, poor ones included, though some repeat studies have found smaller effects. Tim Kasser's research on materialism links strong money and possession goals with lower well-being. Philosophy said it first. Seneca wrote to his friend Lucilius that the poor man is not the one who has too little but the one who craves more. Jesus told his listeners to consider the lilies of the field, which neither toil nor spin. Stoic and Buddhist teachers alike taught holding things loosely. None of this means money is unimportant: earning, keeping and growing still matter, and the earlier principles stand. It means that once you are secure, the most abundant life is usually the most open one: generous, curious, lightly packed and rich in giving.

tales.title: The Man Who Planted Ahead
tales.who: John Chapman, known as Johnny Appleseed
tales.where: Pennsylvania, Ohio and Indiana, USA
tales.source: Land records and recollections of settlers; W. D. Haley, "Johnny Appleseed: A Pioneer Hero", Harper's New Monthly Magazine (1871). Much of the popular legend is folklore.
tales.tale:
A canoe drifts down a wide river, heavy with sacks. Not food. Seeds: apple seeds, thousands of them, washed out of the crushed fruit at cider presses in Pennsylvania. The man at the paddle is thin and barefoot, and he is heading where the settlers have not yet arrived.

His name was John Chapman, born in Leominster, Massachusetts, in 1774. History remembers him as Johnny Appleseed. The legend has given him a cooking pot for a hat and sent him scattering seeds from his pockets like the sower in a parable. The truth is stranger, and more practical.

Chapman did not scatter. He planted nurseries, fenced patches of cleared ground near rivers on the frontier, and he did it a step ahead of the wagons. When families came to claim land, they needed fruit trees, and some land grants even required settlers to plant orchards to make their claims good. There, waiting for them, would be Chapman's young trees, sold for a few pennies each, or for a promise, or for an old coat. Then he moved on, planted again, and came back years later to tend what he had left.

Most of his apples were small and sour, grown from seed rather than grafted. They were for cider and vinegar, which the frontier needed badly, more than for eating. He was, in his way, a businessman, and when he died he held land in more than one place.

But he lived as if he owned nothing. He slept outdoors or by the fires of strangers. He followed the teachings of Emanuel Swedenborg, a Swedish thinker who wrote about heaven. As the stories tell, he tore his books into parts, left a few pages with each family, and swapped them on his next visit. Settlers remembered him reading aloud at their tables, gentle with animals, giving away much of what he had. Some of these stories have surely been polished in the retelling; the heart of them comes from people who knew him.

He died in 1845 near Fort Wayne, Indiana. He never saw most of the orchards his trees became. That was never the point.

A seed in the hand is one seed. The same seed in the ground, given time, becomes a tree, and the tree, given time, makes more seeds than anyone could count. Chapman spent his whole life on the far side of that arithmetic, always planting, always ahead.
tales.reveals: Abundance is a habit of planting ahead, often for people you will never meet. Chapman was not careless with money, but he held it lightly and measured his life by what grew from him.

tales.title: My Brain Is Open
tales.who: Paul Erdős, Hungarian mathematician, and the friends who opened their homes to him
tales.where: Budapest, and homes and universities in many countries
tales.source: Paul Hoffman, The Man Who Loved Only Numbers (1998); Bruce Schechter, My Brain Is Open (1998); obituaries (1996)
tales.tale:
A knock at the door, late at night. On the step stands a small, thin man in a rumpled suit, holding one half-empty suitcase and a plastic shopping bag. He does not say hello. He says, as the story is always told: My brain is open.

He meant: let us do mathematics. Paul Erdős, born in Budapest in 1913, had no house, no wife, no car, and for most of his life no permanent job. What he had was problems, beautiful puzzles about numbers and patterns, and friends all over the world who would open their doors to him. He would arrive, work with his host day and night for a week, sleeping a few hours, drinking strong coffee, and then move on. To the next city. The next door. The next open brain.

He wrote around 1,500 papers with more than 500 different partners, more than almost any mathematician who has ever lived. Mathematicians still measure their closeness to him with the Erdős number. If you wrote a paper with him, your number is one; if you wrote with someone who did, it is two.

Money passed through his hands like water through a basket. When he won the Wolf Prize in 1983, one of the great awards in mathematics, his share was 50,000 dollars. He is reported to have kept 720 dollars and given away the rest, much of it to a scholarship in his parents' memory. He paid prizes from his own pocket to anyone who solved the problems he posed. His biographer Paul Hoffman tells of a young man who needed money to begin at Harvard. Erdős lent it. When the student later tried to repay him, Erdős told him to give it instead to someone else in need.

He was not a saint. He took pills to stay awake, and his friends worried. He leaned on others to cook, drive and wash his clothes, and their kindness was part of what made his freedom possible. A suitcase life is easier when the whole world keeps a spare bed for you.

But what he gave was enormous: his time, his ideas and his full attention, poured freely into hundreds of other minds. He died in 1996 in Warsaw, at a mathematics meeting, still working.

He owned almost nothing. He gave away almost everything. And no one who knew him seems to remember him as poor.
tales.reveals: Abundance can be a way of living rather than a balance: giving time, ideas and money freely, and travelling light. Erdős also shows that such freedom rests on a web of other people's generosity, so true abundance is something we hold together.

practice: Plant something this week that you will not harvest soon. It could be a tree or seedling, a small savings deposit for a child, or a skill taught to a younger colleague.
Give away three things you have not used in a year to someone who will use them, and notice how it feels.
Pay forward one kindness: help someone the way someone once helped you, and ask only that they do the same for another.
Journal two lists: what you have more than enough of (time, skill, food, attention) and who could use some of it. Choose one name and act.
principles.shadow: Talk of abundance can turn into magical thinking, careless spending or a refusal to plan. A free-spirited life can become living off others with nothing given back. Live open-handed from a secure base: build your reserve first, then give and share freely from it.
